title: The Odyssey
author: Homer
setting: Mediterranean and Ithaca
hook: A missing king, a waiting wife, and a voyage where one boast can ruin everything.

characters.name: Odysseus
characters.role: Clever traveller and king of Ithaca

scenes.title: A home without its king
scenes.text: Once upon a time, on the island of Ithaca, a queen waited for a king who had not returned from war. Strangers filled his house, eating his food and demanding that Penelope choose a new husband.

scenes.title: The son must grow up
scenes.text: Their son, Telemachus, had grown up with stories instead of a father. Encouraged by Athena, he sailed to seek news. Someone in the wide world might know whether Odysseus still lived.

scenes.title: Penelope buys time
scenes.text: Penelope promised to choose when she finished weaving a burial cloth. Each night she secretly undid the day's work. While her son searched the sea, she fought to keep their home.

scenes.title: Nobody escapes
scenes.text: Far away, Odysseus and his men were trapped in a one-eyed giant's cave. Calling himself Nobody, he blinded Polyphemus and escaped beneath the sheep. His clever plan worked—until pride interrupted.

scenes.title: The name becomes a weapon
scenes.text: As his ship pulled away, Odysseus shouted his real name. Now the giant could ask his father, the sea god Poseidon, for revenge. The road home became much longer.

scenes.title: Temptations at sea
scenes.text: The travellers met Circe's enchantments, the Sirens' deadly song, and monsters guarding narrow waters. Every escape brought another danger; courage alone could not keep the whole crew alive.

scenes.title: The warning meets appetite
scenes.text: Despite a warning, the hungry men killed the Sun god's cattle. Disaster followed, and Odysseus lost his companions. The man who had led a fleet now faced the sea alone.

scenes.title: The stranger receives hospitality
scenes.text: After years detained by Calypso, Odysseus finally reached the Phaeacians. They welcomed the battered stranger. For once, a shore offered listeners and food rather than another trap.
scenes.cue: A STORY can open a way home

scenes.title: The listener offers a ship
scenes.text: Odysseus told his hosts what he had endured. They gave him passage home. But reaching Ithaca would not be enough: strangers still ruled the household he hoped to enter.

scenes.title: A hidden return
scenes.text: Athena disguised him as a beggar. He met Telemachus in secret, and father and son planned together. The missing king was home, but almost nobody knew it.

scenes.title: The household must recognise him
scenes.text: His old dog recognised him; later, his nurse knew the scar on his leg. Penelope remained cautious. After so many false hopes, she needed more than a stranger's claim.

scenes.title: The bow and the bed
scenes.text: Odysseus strung his bow, defeated the suitors, and faced Penelope's final test: their bed, built around a living olive tree. He knew its secret. At last, the waiting wife knew her husband.

question: What proves Odysseus is truly Penelope's husband?
answer: His knowledge of their marriage bed, built around a living olive tree.
note: Traditional approximate date; oral composition and authorship are debated. Scenes follow the remembered journey rather than the epic's nonlinear telling.

quotes.text: there is a time for many words and there is a time for sleep.
quotes.context: Odysseus addressing Alcinous, Book XI; S. H. Butcher and Andrew Lang translation.
quotes.meaning: Even the great storyteller must pause: remember the voyage inside a hospitable listener's hall.

title: Antigone
author: Sophocles
setting: Thebes
hook: A sister carries a handful of earth toward a king's forbidden grave.

scenes.title: Two brothers dead
scenes.text: In ancient Thebes, two brothers had killed each other in civil war. King Creon honoured one and denied burial to the other. Their sister Antigone could not leave Polynices unburied.

scenes.title: The sister sees the danger
scenes.text: Antigone asked Ismene to help. Her sister feared the king's punishment and refused. Now Antigone had to choose: obey the law, or carry out the sacred duty she believed came first.

scenes.title: The forbidden burial
scenes.text: She covered her brother's body with earth. Guards caught her, and Creon demanded an answer. Antigone admitted what she had done; she would not pretend that fear had changed her belief.

scenes.title: The deed cannot be hidden by denial
scenes.text: Creon expected obedience, but the prisoner offered no apology. To Antigone, a king's order could not cancel obligations to the dead. The argument became a struggle neither would surrender.
scenes.cue: THE DEED CANNOT BE HIDDEN BY DENIAL

scenes.title: Ismene wants to share the blame
scenes.text: Ismene now wanted to share her sister's punishment. Antigone refused to let her claim a deed she had not helped perform. Even affection could not make their earlier choices disappear.
scenes.cue: LOVE does not rewrite the deed

scenes.title: Authority grows afraid of listening
scenes.text: The more Antigone resisted, the more Creon treated resistance as a threat to his rule. Other voices were closing in around him. Would he hear advice, or only disloyalty?

scenes.title: The king refuses
scenes.text: Creon's son Haemon loved Antigone and urged his father to reconsider. The king refused. Antigone would be shut inside a rocky tomb, alive and cut off from the city.

scenes.title: A son risks disagreement
scenes.text: Haemon tried to explain that a ruler could learn from others. Creon heard a son challenging his authority. Their conversation broke apart, and Haemon left with a terrible warning.

scenes.title: The city has another voice
scenes.text: Haemon reported that people quietly sympathised with Antigone. Fear kept those opinions from reaching the king openly. The silence around Creon was making his certainty dangerously easy.
scenes.cue: RULING does not mean refusing to hear

scenes.title: The warning arrives
scenes.text: The prophet Tiresias brought a warning: the gods rejected the city's offerings. At last Creon gave way. He would bury Polynices and release Antigone—but time had been passing.

scenes.title: The rescuer is finally on the road
scenes.text: Creon hurried to repair what he had ordered. The earth could cover the brother's body; the tomb could be opened. Yet a changed command could not guarantee a living prisoner.
scenes.cue: THE RESCUER IS FINALLY ON THE ROAD

scenes.title: Too late to save them
scenes.text: Antigone had hanged herself. Haemon died by suicide, and his mother Eurydice followed. Creon survived, surrounded by losses his late change of heart could no longer prevent.

question: Why does Antigone oppose Creon?
answer: She places sacred obligations to the dead above the king's burial prohibition.
note: First performance traditionally dated around 441 BCE; not a modern publication date.

quotes.text: Love, and not hatred, is the part for me.
quotes.context: Antigone answering Creon; Lewis Campbell translation.
quotes.meaning: Her obligations arise from kinship and love, while Creon frames loyalty through enemies.

title: Beowulf
author: Anonymous
setting: Denmark and Geatland
hook: A feast hall goes silent, and a stranger volunteers to wait inside it after dark.

characters.name: Unferth
characters.role: Danish courtier who questions Beowulf’s boast

scenes.title: The hall falls silent
scenes.text: Long ago in Denmark, King Hrothgar's great hall stood empty at night. The monster Grendel had turned its feasts into slaughter. Across the sea, a warrior named Beowulf heard the news.

scenes.title: The stranger asks for the fight
scenes.text: Beowulf sailed from Geatland with his companions and offered to face the attacker. Hrothgar welcomed him. That night, the hall would have guests again—and someone waiting for Grendel.
scenes.cue: THE STRANGER ASKS FOR THE FIGHT

scenes.title: The boast must become action
scenes.text: Beowulf promised to fight without a sword, matching the monster's bare strength. Such a promise sounded magnificent at a feast. In the darkness, he would have to make it true.

scenes.title: The boast meets a remembering rival
scenes.text: Unferth challenged the newcomer's reputation, recalling an old swimming contest. Beowulf answered with his own account. Words settled nothing about Grendel; the coming night would judge the boast.
scenes.cue: THE BOAST MEETS A REMEMBERING RIVAL

scenes.title: Strength without a sword
scenes.text: Grendel entered the hall and found a grip he could not escape. Beowulf tore away the monster's arm. Mortally wounded, Grendel fled, leaving the hall with an astonishing trophy.

scenes.title: The trophy cannot end the danger
scenes.text: The Danes celebrated beneath that hanging arm. But Grendel had a mother, and victory had given her a reason to attack. The hall's restored peace lasted only briefly.
scenes.cue: THE TROPHY CANNOT END THE DANGER

scenes.title: Beneath the mere
scenes.text: After her revenge raid, Beowulf followed Grendel's mother to a dark lake. He plunged beneath the water and entered her hall. This time, his own sword failed him.

scenes.title: The hero enters another household
scenes.text: A giant sword in the underwater hall gave him another chance. He killed his opponent and returned to the surface. The waiting warriors saw their lost hero emerge alive.

scenes.title: Victory becomes kingship
scenes.text: Years passed. Beowulf returned home and eventually became king. His youthful victories became stories people remembered—until a stolen cup woke a dragon and brought danger to his own people.
scenes.cue: A HERO must also protect a people

scenes.title: The last battle
scenes.text: The ageing king went to fight the dragon. Most companions fled, but young Wiglaf stayed. Together they killed it; the victory came with a wound Beowulf could not survive.

scenes.title: The young warrior remembers his debt
scenes.text: Wiglaf remembered the gifts and trust his king had given him. When the others ran, that debt kept him beside Beowulf. Loyalty arrived where a whole company had failed.
scenes.cue: THE YOUNG WARRIOR REMEMBERS HIS DEBT

scenes.title: The funeral mound
scenes.text: The Geats raised a funeral mound above the sea and buried their king's treasure with him. They mourned the protector they had lost, afraid of what enemies might do next.

question: Which warrior stays with Beowulf against the dragon?
answer: Wiglaf. His loyalty contrasts with the warriors who flee.
note: Composition is uncertain. The manuscript date provides the timeline anchor; the story is set much earlier.

quotes.text: Weird often saveth
quotes.context: Beowulf's account of the swimming contest; J. Lesslie Hall translation, section IX. The sentence continues with the undoomed hero's courage.
quotes.meaning: Fate and brave action work together in the hero's understanding of survival.

title: The Canterbury Tales
author: Geoffrey Chaucer
setting: A pilgrimage from London to Canterbury
hook: Travellers share a road, but their stories soon start arguing with one another.

scenes.title: At the Tabard
scenes.text: One spring, pilgrims gathered at the Tabard Inn before travelling to Canterbury. Their host, Harry Bailly, proposed a storytelling contest. The journey would have company, entertainment, and a judge.

scenes.title: A reward gives the voices a frame
scenes.text: The best storyteller would win a supper paid for by the others. With that prize in view, each traveller gained a chance to hold everyone's attention. Who would tell the next tale?
scenes.cue: A REWARD GIVES THE VOICES A FRAME

scenes.title: The portraits already tell stories
scenes.text: A knight, a miller, a pardoner, a wife from Bath: the company brought different trades, clothes, manners, and ambitions. Before they spoke, the narrator was already noticing their contradictions.

scenes.title: The storyteller can be judged too
scenes.text: The stories would reveal more than imagined adventures. A teller's choices could expose pride, prejudice, or private experience. On this road, the audience could answer back.
scenes.cue: THE STORYTELLER CAN BE JUDGED TOO

scenes.title: Order meets disruption
scenes.text: The Knight began with noble rivals competing for love. Then the drunken Miller insisted on telling his own tale: trickery and desire in a carpenter's household. The dignified order collapsed.

scenes.title: The interrupted order stays broken
scenes.text: The Miller's story provoked another answer. The pilgrims were no longer simply taking polite turns; one tale could challenge the people and values behind another.

scenes.title: Who holds authority?
scenes.text: The Wife of Bath spoke about her five marriages and challenged men who claimed authority over women. Then her tale asked a knight what women most desired.

scenes.title: Experience answers the authorities
scenes.text: Her own experience stood against learned rules quoted by others. She refused to let authorities speak for every marriage. The listeners had to meet a woman prepared to answer them.

scenes.title: The answer is a choice
scenes.text: In her tale, the knight learned that women desire control over their own lives. His final test was practical: would he let his wife make her own choice?

scenes.title: A sermon against greed
scenes.text: The Pardoner confessed his greed, then preached against it. In his story, three men sought Death, found gold, and plotted against each other. Their treasure became the means of their destruction.

scenes.title: The sermon catches its speaker
scenes.text: After that warning, the Pardoner tried to sell his pardons to the company. His preaching and his behaviour collided in front of the very people he hoped to profit from.

scenes.title: An unfinished journey
scenes.text: The surviving collection never completes the promised contest. Its lasting company is a crowd of competing voices: follow the pilgrimage, and keep noticing who speaks through each story.

question: Why is this a frame narrative?
answer: A pilgrimage and storytelling contest form the outer story that contains the individual tales.

quotes.text: Whan that Aprill with his shoures soote
quotes.context: General Prologue, opening line; Middle English.
quotes.meaning: Spring stirs the desire to travel, placing the individual tales within a shared pilgrimage.

title: The Spanish Tragedy
author: Thomas Kyd
setting: Spain and Portugal
hook: A father finds his murdered son, then turns a court entertainment into something terrifyingly real.

scenes.title: A ghost watches
scenes.text: After a war between Spain and Portugal, the dead Don Andrea watched the living with the figure of Revenge. On earth, court celebrations hid rivalries that the war had not settled.

scenes.title: The war leaves a private rivalry
scenes.text: The captured Portuguese prince Balthazar wanted Bel-imperia. She loved Horatio instead. Her brother Lorenzo supported Balthazar, and a private love affair became a dangerous obstacle to powerful men.
scenes.cue: THE WAR LEAVES A PRIVATE RIVALRY

scenes.title: Love in the garden
scenes.text: Bel-imperia and Horatio met in a garden, hoping for a moment together. Lorenzo and Balthazar's men attacked. Their meeting ended with Horatio murdered and Bel-imperia carried away.

scenes.title: The garden holds a murdered son
scenes.text: Hieronimo found his son's body hanging in the garden. The father who served the court's justice now needed justice himself. Grief gave him a question the court did not want answered.
scenes.cue: THE GARDEN HOLDS A MURDERED SON

scenes.title: The father reads the evidence
scenes.text: The signs of violence could not tell Hieronimo everything. He searched for the people behind his son's death, torn between terrible suspicion and the need for proof.

scenes.title: The letter offers dangerous knowledge
scenes.text: Bel-imperia secretly sent a letter naming the killers. Hieronimo had evidence, but using it meant accusing men protected by rank. Knowing the truth did not make speaking it safe.

scenes.title: Justice is blocked
scenes.text: His attempts to obtain justice met obstruction. Hieronimo's grief deepened, and the court treated his distress as madness. The door he needed kept closing.

scenes.title: The appeal reaches a closed system
scenes.text: Lorenzo guarded his position while Hieronimo struggled to reach the king. An appeal through official channels offered little protection when powerful people could block its path.
scenes.cue: THE APPEAL REACHES A CLOSED SYSTEM

scenes.title: Isabella cannot bear the garden
scenes.text: Hieronimo's wife Isabella could not endure the place where Horatio died. She destroyed the garden and died by suicide. The family's loss had spread beyond the murdered son.

scenes.title: A play within the play
scenes.text: Hieronimo proposed a play for the court, recruiting the guilty nobles as actors. They agreed to the entertainment. Bel-imperia knew that the performance would carry another purpose.

scenes.title: The actors do not know the whole play
scenes.text: The actors raised real weapons where the audience expected imitation. Balthazar and Lorenzo were killed; Bel-imperia also killed herself. Applause could no longer separate theatre from death.
scenes.cue: THE ACTORS DO NOT KNOW THE WHOLE PLAY

scenes.title: The final silence
scenes.text: Hieronimo exposed the revenge behind the performance, then died after further violence. Don Andrea's watching ghost finally received his promised satisfaction; the living court was left in ruin.

question: How does Hieronimo carry out his revenge?
answer: He uses a play within the play, replacing theatrical violence with real killings.
note: Approximate composition or early performance range; dating is uncertain.

quotes.text: While then ile fit you
quotes.context: Hieronimo, Act IV, preparing the fatal play; original spelling of the linked early text.
quotes.meaning: The apparently helpful theatre maker turns performance into revenge.

title: The Faerie Queene
author: Edmund Spenser
setting: An imagined realm of knights and trials
hook: A knight follows Truth into a world where evil often wears a trustworthy face.

scenes.title: Truth and its knight
scenes.text: Once upon a time, a knight bearing a red cross rode beside Una, a woman representing Truth. Her parents needed rescue from a dragon. Before that battle, he would face other dangers.

scenes.title: A guide can appear virtuous
scenes.text: Their path brought them to Archimago, a magician disguised as a holy man. His welcome seemed safe. Behind that appearance, he was preparing false visions to separate the companions.

scenes.title: False appearances
scenes.text: The knight believed the deception and abandoned Una. Duessa, another false guide, won his trust. He had set out to defend Truth and was now travelling without her.

scenes.title: The false lady wins attention
scenes.text: Duessa's beautiful appearance concealed what she really was. Following her led the knight deeper into danger. His difficulty was no longer simply fighting enemies: he could not recognise them.

scenes.title: Despair turns guilt against the knight
scenes.text: After rescue from the giant Orgoglio, the knight encountered Despair. His past failures now seemed like reasons to give up. The next attack came through words rather than a weapon.
scenes.cue: TRUTH resists the voice of despair

scenes.title: Despair makes a persuasive argument
scenes.text: Despair argued that death could end the knight's guilt. The wounded man nearly accepted. Una intervened, refusing to let his mistakes become the end of his journey.

scenes.title: Fall and restoration
scenes.text: Una brought him to the House of Holiness. There he learned repentance, faith, and the strength to begin again. Rescue required more than being pulled out of a giant's prison.

scenes.title: Holiness must be restored before battle
scenes.text: Restored, the knight prepared to face the dragon at last. The journey had shown how easily courage could follow the wrong guide. Now he returned to the duty he had abandoned.
scenes.cue: HOLINESS MUST BE RESTORED BEFORE BATTLE

scenes.title: The dragon defeated
scenes.text: The dragon battle lasted three days. The knight survived terrible wounds and finally killed it, freeing Una's parents. The red cross had reached its promised trial.

scenes.title: Guyon tests appetite
scenes.text: Other books followed other knights. Guyon, representing Temperance, faced pleasures that invited him to surrender self-control. His challenge led toward the enchanted Bower of Bliss.

scenes.title: Different virtues face different temptations
scenes.text: Britomart pursued a vision of love while defending chastity; other knights tested friendship, justice, and courtesy. Their paths crossed, and no single victory solved every moral danger.

scenes.title: The other virtues
scenes.text: The unfinished poem leaves a wide landscape of quests. Remember its central warning: a shining costume or persuasive voice can mislead a brave traveller before the sword is ever drawn.

question: What does Una represent?
answer: Truth. Redcrosse's journey requires learning to remain faithful to her.

quotes.text: A Gentle Knight was pricking on the plaine
quotes.context: Book I, Canto I, opening line.
quotes.meaning: A knight riding across a plain begins the outward journey that also represents a moral trial.

title: Doctor Faustus
author: Christopher Marlowe
setting: Wittenberg and a supernatural world
hook: A brilliant scholar buys extraordinary power—and watches his remaining time run out.

scenes.title: Knowledge is not enough
scenes.text: In a university town, Doctor Faustus had mastered celebrated subjects and still felt unsatisfied. He wanted knowledge and power beyond ordinary limits. Magic seemed to offer the door he was seeking.

scenes.title: The scholar wants an unlimited door
scenes.text: Books became instructions for summoning spirits. Faustus imagined command over the world, far greater than the respect a scholar could earn. He began reaching for a bargain he barely understood.
scenes.cue: THE SCHOLAR WANTS AN UNLIMITED DOOR

scenes.title: The bargain
scenes.text: He agreed to give Lucifer his soul in exchange for twenty-four years of Mephistopheles' service. The promise sounded enormous. Its price would fall due when the years ended.

scenes.title: The warning comes from the servant
scenes.text: Mephistopheles warned that separation from God was itself hell. Faustus heard someone who already suffered the cost. Yet he kept treating that warning as something he could set aside.
scenes.cue: THE WARNING COMES FROM THE SERVANT

scenes.title: The devil remembers what was lost
scenes.text: The spirit remembered the happiness he had lost. His account offered Faustus a glimpse beyond the impressive appearance of supernatural power. The scholar preferred the promise to the warning.

scenes.title: The signature meets resistance
scenes.text: When Faustus signed in blood, even the blood resisted flowing. The contract was completed anyway. From then on, time was part of every pleasure he bought.

scenes.title: Power shrinks into spectacle
scenes.text: Faustus travelled and performed wonders, but his grand ambitions often dwindled into tricks and entertainments. The man who wanted limitless mastery spent precious years impressing other people.

scenes.title: The great promise becomes small tricks
scenes.text: He mocked opponents and delighted spectators with supernatural displays. Each little triumph used the same bargain. None enlarged the twenty-four years written into it.
scenes.cue: THE GREAT PROMISE BECOMES SMALL TRICKS

scenes.title: Helen becomes another spectacle
scenes.text: He summoned an appearance of Helen of Troy and turned toward its beauty. Another dazzling spectacle distracted him from the question waiting beneath everything: could he still repent?
scenes.cue: BEAUTY does not cancel the bargain

scenes.title: Repentance postponed
scenes.text: Good advice and thoughts of repentance returned, but Faustus delayed or turned away. What seemed possible tomorrow became harder to choose today. The deadline kept approaching.

scenes.title: The last hour cannot be stretched
scenes.text: In the last hour, he begged time to slow and the clock to stop. He imagined escape from the punishment he feared. The ordinary movement of minutes now felt unbearable.
scenes.cue: THE LAST HOUR CANNOT BE STRETCHED

scenes.title: The final hour
scenes.text: Midnight came, and devils carried Faustus away. His learning had opened many doors, but he had repeatedly refused the one that might have changed his end.

question: What is the central bargain?
answer: Twenty-four years of supernatural service in exchange for Faustus's soul.
note: Composition is disputed; the supplied notes use c. 1592. A-text published 1604 and B-text 1616.

quotes.text: Was this the face that launch'd a thousand ships
quotes.context: Faustus addressing the apparition of Helen, late in the play.
quotes.meaning: His language sounds magnificent, but the spectacle distracts him from his approaching reckoning.

title: Othello
author: William Shakespeare
setting: Venice and Cyprus
hook: A trusted friend plants a suspicion, and a loving husband starts mistaking lies for proof.

scenes.title: A marriage defended
scenes.text: In Venice, Othello and Desdemona had married despite her father's opposition. Othello, a respected commander, defended their love before the authorities. Then duty called the couple to Cyprus.

scenes.title: The marriage already needs defence
scenes.text: Desdemona chose to stand beside her husband. They had survived an open accusation against their marriage. The greater danger would arrive from someone Othello believed was his friend.

scenes.title: The honest mask
scenes.text: Iago resented Othello and concealed his hatred behind loyalty. Othello trusted his advice. That trust gave Iago room to shape what his commander would think he saw.

scenes.title: The helpful voice prepares the wound
scenes.text: Iago sounded helpful while studying each person's weakness. He did not need to make Othello jealous at once. First he needed situations that could later be made to look suspicious.
scenes.cue: THE HELPFUL VOICE PREPARES THE WOUND

scenes.title: Iago opens the trap
scenes.text: He drew the disappointed suitor Roderigo into his schemes. Money, resentment, and hope made Roderigo useful. Around Othello, Iago was quietly assembling people he could manipulate.

scenes.title: A ruined night creates an opening
scenes.text: Iago encouraged Cassio to drink, then helped provoke a brawl. Othello dismissed Cassio from his post. Now Cassio had a reason to seek Desdemona's help—and Iago had a story to twist.
scenes.cue: A RUINED NIGHT CREATES AN OPENING

scenes.title: The handkerchief
scenes.text: Desdemona asked Othello to restore Cassio. Iago suggested that her concern concealed an affair. Then her handkerchief, a gift from Othello, went missing.

scenes.title: The token leaves its first meaning
scenes.text: Emilia picked it up, and Iago used it in his deception. A token of love became apparent evidence against its owner. Othello did not know the route it had taken.
scenes.cue: THE TOKEN LEAVES ITS FIRST MEANING

scenes.title: The questions do the damage
scenes.text: Iago offered hints, staged appearances, and false explanations. Othello began demanding certainty from the very man inventing the suspicion. Desdemona's innocence could not compete with the manufactured proof.

scenes.title: Jealousy becomes murder
scenes.text: Believing Desdemona unfaithful, Othello killed her in their bed. The wife who had chosen him could not make him hear the truth before his jealousy became an irreversible act.

scenes.title: The witness will not remain silent
scenes.text: Emilia recognised what the handkerchief had been used to do. She spoke despite Iago's threats and exposed his lies. Her husband killed her, but he could not silence the revelation.
scenes.cue: THE WITNESS WILL NOT REMAIN SILENT

scenes.title: The truth arrives
scenes.text: Othello finally understood Desdemona's innocence and died by suicide. Iago was taken for punishment. The truth arrived, carrying no power to restore the people destroyed before it was heard.

question: Why is the handkerchief so important?
answer: Iago manipulates its movement to make an innocent object appear to prove Desdemona's infidelity.
note: Othello is described as a Moor; the play does not establish a precise modern nationality or religious biography.

quotes.text: I am not what I am.
quotes.context: Iago, Act I, scene 1.
quotes.meaning: The manipulator announces the distance between his appearance and his purpose.

title: Macbeth
author: William Shakespeare
setting: Scotland
hook: Three strangers promise a soldier a crown; reaching for it costs him every peaceful night.

scenes.title: The prophecy
scenes.text: On a wild Scottish heath, Macbeth and Banquo met three witches after battle. They predicted that Macbeth would become king. Then part of their greeting unexpectedly came true.

scenes.title: Two futures stand beside one another
scenes.text: The witches also promised that Banquo's descendants would be kings. Macbeth heard a splendid future for himself and a troubling future for his companion. Both predictions travelled home with him.
scenes.cue: TWO FUTURES STAND BESIDE ONE ANOTHER

scenes.title: The hesitation before the act
scenes.text: King Duncan trusted Macbeth and came to his castle as a guest. Macbeth knew what murder would violate. Desire for the crown pulled him toward an act he still feared.
scenes.cue: KNOWING the wrong does not stop the choice

scenes.title: The letter carries temptation home
scenes.text: Lady Macbeth read his letter about the prophecy and urged him to seize the chance. When he hesitated, she pressed his resolve. Together they planned Duncan's death beneath their own roof.

scenes.title: Duncan is murdered
scenes.text: Macbeth murdered the sleeping king. The guards were blamed, and Duncan's sons fled in fear. Their flight helped Macbeth take the throne he had imagined on the heath.

scenes.title: The guest is also their king
scenes.text: The crown did not undo the night. Duncan had been his guest and his king; Macbeth could not make those obligations disappear. Safety now depended on hiding one crime with others.
scenes.cue: THE GUEST IS ALSO THEIR KING

scenes.title: The crown makes another man frightening
scenes.text: Banquo knew the prophecy, and his promised descendants troubled Macbeth. Macbeth arranged his murder. Banquo died, but his son Fleance escaped, leaving the prediction beyond the new king's control.
scenes.cue: THE CROWN MAKES ANOTHER MAN FRIGHTENING

scenes.title: A ghost at the feast
scenes.text: At a royal feast, Macbeth saw Banquo's ghost in his seat. The guests could not see what terrified him. His public performance as king began to break apart.

scenes.title: The crown brings no rest
scenes.text: Macbeth ordered further violence, including the killing of Macduff's family. Every attempt to secure the crown produced more enemies. Far from resting, he kept defending what murder had gained.

scenes.title: False security
scenes.text: The witches offered reassuring predictions: no man born of woman would defeat him, and he was safe until Birnam Wood moved. Macbeth treated their strange conditions as impossible threats.

scenes.title: The queen cannot wash away memory
scenes.text: Lady Macbeth walked in her sleep, trying to wash imagined blood from her hands. She later died, leaving Macbeth to face the approaching battle without the partner who had urged him onward.
scenes.cue: THE QUEEN CANNOT WASH AWAY MEMORY

scenes.title: The promises unravel
scenes.text: Soldiers advanced carrying branches from Birnam Wood. Macduff revealed he had been delivered by a surgical birth and killed Macbeth. The promises had hidden their danger inside the words he trusted.

question: How does Birnam Wood move?
answer: Soldiers camouflage themselves with branches, fulfilling the prophecy in an unexpected way.

quotes.text: Fair is foul, and foul is fair:
quotes.context: The witches, Act I, scene 1.
quotes.meaning: The opening inversion prepares us for promises that make evil appear desirable.

title: The Tempest
author: William Shakespeare
setting: A Mediterranean island
hook: A ship breaks apart in a storm, but someone on the island has planned every wave.

scenes.title: The manufactured storm
scenes.text: Near a lonely island, a storm threw a royal ship into panic. On shore, Miranda pleaded for the passengers. Her father Prospero assured her that his magic had kept them safe.

scenes.title: The storm has a hidden director
scenes.text: Prospero had ordered the storm through the spirit Ariel. Years earlier, his brother Antonio had stolen his dukedom and driven him into exile. Now that brother was within reach.
scenes.cue: THE STORM HAS A HIDDEN DIRECTOR

scenes.title: A father controls the telling
scenes.text: Prospero told Miranda how they had reached the island. Her childhood home was also her father's place of banishment. The strangers from the ship carried the past he had kept from her.

scenes.title: Two different kinds of service
scenes.text: Ariel longed for freedom after serving Prospero. Caliban, the island's inhabitant, bitterly resisted him. Beneath the magician's commands were different histories of rescue, possession, and forced service.
scenes.cue: ASK who is allowed to leave

scenes.title: Love under supervision
scenes.text: Miranda met Ferdinand, the king's son, and they fell in love. Prospero made Ferdinand carry logs. The young man accepted the labour, hoping to prove his devotion.

scenes.title: Love enters a planned encounter
scenes.text: Their meeting looked accidental to the lovers, but Prospero had helped arrange it. Miranda discovered a world beyond her father. Her father still watched the path toward it.

scenes.title: Two plots
scenes.text: Elsewhere, Antonio tempted Sebastian to murder his brother, King Alonso. Caliban recruited two drunken shipwrecked men against Prospero. The island now held more than one plan for taking power.

scenes.title: The island contains competing claims
scenes.text: Caliban promised to show his allies the island's resources. To him, Prospero was an intruder to be overthrown. The comic plot carried a serious anger beneath its drunken confusion.

scenes.title: The masque is interrupted
scenes.text: Prospero presented a magical celebration for the lovers, then abruptly stopped it when he remembered Caliban's plot. Even his beautiful pageant could not keep danger outside the moment.

scenes.title: The choice to forgive
scenes.text: With his enemies in his power, Prospero considered revenge. Ariel's account of their suffering moved him toward mercy. He chose forgiveness and prepared to reveal himself.

scenes.title: The magic must end with the judgement
scenes.text: Prospero recovered his dukedom and accepted Ferdinand's marriage to Miranda. Ariel's service was ending. To leave the island, Prospero would also have to release the power that governed it.
scenes.cue: THE MAGIC MUST END WITH THE JUDGEMENT

scenes.title: Magic surrendered
scenes.text: He gave up his magic and freed Ariel. A ship waited to carry the company home. The man who had directed their ordeal now asked the audience for his own release.

question: What does Prospero give up at the end?
answer: His magic and control over Ariel, as part of moving from revenge toward reconciliation.

quotes.text: We are such stuff
quotes.context: Prospero, Act IV, scene 1; the sentence continues with dreams.
quotes.meaning: After the masque dissolves, he connects theatrical illusion with the fragility of human life.

title: Paradise Lost
author: John Milton
setting: Hell, Heaven and Eden
hook: A defeated rebel chooses revenge, and two people in a garden become his target.

scenes.title: Defeat in Heaven
scenes.text: Before human history, Satan and his followers rebelled against God and were cast into Hell. Defeat did not quiet their leader. He began turning their ruin into a call for another struggle.

scenes.title: The rebel makes defeat sound heroic
scenes.text: Satan's speeches gave his followers a story of injured greatness. He could not restore Heaven by speaking, but he could persuade them to keep resisting rather than accept defeat.
scenes.cue: THE REBEL MAKES DEFEAT SOUND HEROIC

scenes.title: The journey needs a target
scenes.text: He learned of a newly created world and humankind. If he could not overthrow God, perhaps he could damage what God loved. His next journey acquired a target.

scenes.title: The council divides imagined remedies
scenes.text: The fallen angels debated renewed war, waiting, and other responses. Their council settled on corrupting God's new creation. Satan undertook the journey himself, crossing the wilderness beyond Hell.

scenes.title: The garden and the warning
scenes.text: In Eden, Adam and Eve lived among abundant gifts. One prohibition remained: they must not eat from the Tree of Knowledge. Freedom included the possibility of disobedience.

scenes.title: The garden contains a choice
scenes.text: The garden's beauty did not make its inhabitants incapable of error. They could choose, and warnings had been given. Satan needed to turn that freedom toward his own revenge.

scenes.title: The serpent persuades
scenes.text: Disguised through the serpent, Satan approached Eve while she worked apart from Adam. He praised her and argued that the forbidden fruit could raise her beyond her present condition.

scenes.title: The serpent separates language from intention
scenes.text: The serpent made disobedience sound like discovery. Its flattering language concealed the speaker's purpose. Eve trusted the promised gain and ate, then carried the fruit to Adam.
scenes.cue: THE SERPENT SEPARATES LANGUAGE FROM INTENTION

scenes.title: The promised change becomes shame
scenes.text: The promised elevation brought shame, fear, and disturbed desire. Their eyes had changed, but the change was not the freedom Satan had advertised. The garden no longer felt the same.
scenes.cue: THE PROMISE changes after the act

scenes.title: Adam chooses to follow
scenes.text: Adam understood that Eve had disobeyed. Unwilling to lose her, he chose to eat too. Love became part of his reason for joining a choice he knew was wrong.

scenes.title: Blame cannot rebuild the garden
scenes.text: The pair accused each other and faced judgement. Blame could not undo the act. Gradually, remorse and the possibility of repentance offered a way beyond their first bitter quarrel.

scenes.title: Leaving with hope
scenes.text: They left Eden together. Michael's revelations gave Adam a future containing suffering and the hope of redemption. Paradise was lost, but the human story still had a road ahead.

question: Why does Adam eat the fruit?
answer: He knowingly follows Eve, unable to bear separation from her; his choice remains disobedience.
note: Combines the accounts in Literature Part 1 and Literature part 3. Ten books in 1667; twelve in 1674.

quotes.text: The mind is its own place
quotes.context: Satan, Book I.
quotes.meaning: Satan claims inner independence; remember that the poem also exposes the pride within his claim.

title: To His Coy Mistress
author: Andrew Marvell
setting: An imagined conversation between lovers
hook: A lover begins with endless time, then uses a ticking clock to press his invitation.

scenes.title: If time were unlimited
scenes.text: Imagine a man addressing a woman who has not agreed to his advances. He begins gently: with limitless time, there would be no need to hurry. That promise opens his argument.

scenes.title: The impossible beginning sounds generous
scenes.text: He imagines centuries for courtship and distant places for their lives. Such patience sounds generous. But this enormous world exists only inside the speaker's persuasive fantasy.

scenes.title: The exaggerations serve persuasion
scenes.text: His extravagant devotion stretches across ages. The exaggeration helps us hear how much he claims to value her. Soon, however, he will take that abundance of time away.

scenes.title: The praise measures a fantasy
scenes.text: He assigns immense stretches of time to praising her beauty. The imagined courtship could last almost forever. Its impossible scale prepares the sudden turn waiting in the next movement.

scenes.title: But time pursues us
scenes.text: Now he brings in time rushing behind them. Human lives are short, he argues, and death approaches. The leisurely opening closes like a door.

scenes.title: The body enters the argument
scenes.text: He pictures what death will do to beauty and desire. The disturbing images put pressure on his listener. Her own reply, however, is never heard in the poem.

scenes.title: The grave is part of the argument
scenes.text: The grave offers neither a lover's embrace nor the life they possess now. By making the alternative frightening, he tries to make immediate intimacy seem urgently reasonable.
scenes.cue: FEAR is being used to persuade

scenes.title: The grave becomes a rhetorical opponent
scenes.text: He treats death as an opponent the lovers should resist together. But he has chosen both sides of the argument: endless waiting or action now. The woman has not set those terms.
scenes.cue: THE GRAVE BECOMES A RHETORICAL OPPONENT

scenes.title: Therefore seize the present
scenes.text: His final movement urges them to gather their energy and seize the present. They cannot stop the sun, he says, but they can make their short lives feel intense.

scenes.title: The final energy remains a proposal
scenes.text: The language imagines two lovers acting together. It remains a proposal from one voice. Nothing in the poem confirms that the woman accepts what he asks.
scenes.cue: THE FINAL ENERGY REMAINS A PROPOSAL

scenes.title: Remember the argument
scenes.text: Follow the argument's changing clock: endless time, approaching death, immediate action. The excitement comes from how quickly the speaker moves the listener between those worlds.

scenes.title: Remember the three turns
scenes.text: The poem ends with the speaker's urgent invitation still hanging in the air. Remember its energy—and the unanswered question of how the silent woman would respond.

question: What are the poem's three argumentative movements?
answer: If we had unlimited time; but we face death; therefore seize the present.
note: Placed by first publication, not likely composition. The mistress never supplies a spoken answer in the poem.

quotes.text: Time's wingèd chariot
quotes.context: The speaker, the poem's middle movement; spelling follows this edition.
quotes.meaning: Time interrupts the fantasy of unlimited courtship. This is the speaker's persuasive argument, not the silent woman's consent.

title: The Way of the World
author: William Congreve
setting: Fashionable London
hook: Two lovers want to marry, but affection must survive an inheritance, a disguise, and a blackmailer.

scenes.title: Love needs consent
scenes.text: In fashionable London, Mirabell wanted to marry Millamant. She wanted him too, but her aunt Lady Wishfort controlled part of her fortune. The lovers needed more than a mutual promise.

scenes.title: The inheritance sits between the lovers
scenes.text: Without her aunt's consent, Millamant risked losing money. Love had become entangled with family power. Mirabell began planning how to reach the woman who held the purse strings.
scenes.cue: THE INHERITANCE SITS BETWEEN THE LOVERS

scenes.title: The past complicates the lovers
scenes.text: Past relationships complicated the scheme, especially Mirabell's former connection with Mrs Fainall. In this circle, private history could become useful information for someone seeking an advantage.

scenes.title: An older woman's wish becomes a lever
scenes.text: Lady Wishfort disliked Mirabell but longed to be admired. He planned to exploit that longing. A supposed distinguished suitor would offer her the attention she wanted.
scenes.cue: AN OLDER WOMAN'S WISH BECOMES A LEVER

scenes.title: The false suitor
scenes.text: The false suitor was Mirabell's servant Waitwell in disguise. Waitwell first married Foible, Lady Wishfort's maid. That hidden marriage would make the promised match impossible.

scenes.title: A servant needs a borrowed rank
scenes.text: With a borrowed name and rank, Waitwell could approach Lady Wishfort as someone she might marry. Foible helped the deception. The household's servants now carried the central plot.
scenes.cue: A SERVANT NEEDS A BORROWED RANK

scenes.title: The proviso scene
scenes.text: Meanwhile, Mirabell and Millamant discussed their own marriage. Instead of merely promising devotion, they negotiated conditions. What room would marriage leave for each person's habits and independence?

scenes.title: The bride insists on private space
scenes.text: Millamant insisted on privacy and freedom within their life together. Mirabell answered with conditions of his own. Their wit became a way to imagine affection without swallowing the other person.
scenes.cue: THE BRIDE INSISTS ON PRIVATE SPACE

scenes.title: The secret is almost exposed
scenes.text: The scheme began to unravel as hidden dealings reached hostile listeners. Lady Wishfort faced embarrassment, and Mirabell's enemies saw a chance to turn the exposure into profit.

scenes.title: Fainall's threat
scenes.text: Fainall threatened to disgrace his wife and demanded control of property. His weapon was reputation: pay him, or let damaging accusations become public. The comedy reached a serious financial trap.

scenes.title: A document defeats the blackmailer
scenes.text: Mirabell produced a legal document protecting Mrs Fainall's property from her husband. It had been arranged before the crisis. The blackmailer's expected prize was beyond his reach.

scenes.title: The document defeats him
scenes.text: Fainall's threat collapsed, and Lady Wishfort consented to the lovers' marriage. Their future rested on affection, negotiated freedom, and a piece of paperwork that wit alone could not replace.

question: What protects Mrs. Fainall's money?
answer: An earlier trust deed placed her property beyond her husband's attempted seizure.

quotes.text: I hate a lover that can dare to think
quotes.context: Millamant, Act IV, the proviso scene; opening of a longer sentence.
quotes.meaning: Her wit insists that affection must allow room for independent life.

title: The Rape of the Lock
author: Alexander Pope
setting: Aristocratic social life around London
hook: At a glittering party, a pair of scissors turns a stolen curl into an epic catastrophe.

scenes.title: An epic dressing table
scenes.text: One morning, Belinda prepared for a fashionable day, surrounded by cosmetics and ornaments. The poem treats her dressing table like a hero's armoury. A social outing begins with epic ceremony.

scenes.title: A morning looks like a ceremony
scenes.text: Her beauty receives the attention that warriors receive before battle. Jars, powders, and jewels become impressive equipment. The narrator's grand manner makes the ordinary ritual wonderfully disproportionate.
scenes.cue: A MORNING LOOKS LIKE A CEREMONY

scenes.title: The machinery is deliberately oversized
scenes.text: Invisible spirits called sylphs guard her, led by Ariel. They give the outing supernatural machinery. Yet the danger concerns reputation and appearance rather than the fate of an actual kingdom.

scenes.title: The guardian sees an uncertain danger
scenes.text: Ariel senses trouble without clearly knowing its form. Belinda enters her polished social world under a warning she cannot fully understand. Somewhere among the compliments, a small disaster waits.
scenes.cue: THE GUARDIAN SEES AN UNCERTAIN DANGER

scenes.title: Cards as warfare
scenes.text: At Hampton Court, Belinda plays a card game against the Baron. The narrator describes it like warfare. Cards move as armies, and a fashionable pastime acquires heroic suspense.

scenes.title: The game imitates a battle
scenes.text: Belinda wins. The splendid battle has produced a social triumph, but the Baron has another object in mind. He wants one of her beautiful locks of hair.

scenes.title: The scissors strike
scenes.text: Clarissa lends him scissors. While Belinda is distracted, he cuts off a curl. The tool is tiny; the outrage that follows will be described on a much grander scale.

scenes.title: A small tool carries the offence
scenes.text: The Baron celebrates his trophy while Belinda discovers the loss. A moment of vanity has become a public offence against her. The party now has opposing sides.
scenes.cue: A SMALL TOOL CARRIES THE OFFENCE

scenes.title: Honour has different meanings
scenes.text: To the Baron, the curl proves conquest. To Belinda, its theft damages honour and appearance. The same little lock carries sharply different meanings for the people arguing over it.
scenes.cue: A SMALL object can carry reputation

scenes.title: Distress becomes combat
scenes.text: Belinda's distress becomes an extravagant battle of gestures, looks, and accusations. The poem borrows the equipment of heroic conflict to show a society furious over a curl.

scenes.title: The advice cannot quiet the quarrel
scenes.text: Clarissa advises them to value good sense and character over passing beauty. The quarrel continues. A sensible speech cannot easily stop people committed to feeling magnificently offended.
scenes.cue: THE ADVICE CANNOT QUIET THE QUARREL

scenes.title: A lock among the stars
scenes.text: The missing lock finally rises, in the poem's fancy, among the stars. Belinda loses her curl but gains poetic fame. The little social incident receives the enormous ending it imagined.

question: Why is this a mock epic?
answer: It applies the grand language and machinery of epic poetry to the comparatively small event of a stolen lock.
note: The historical title uses rape in the sense of taking or seizure. The plot concerns an unauthorised cutting of hair.

quotes.text: What mighty contests rise from trivial things,
quotes.context: Canto I, opening invocation.
quotes.meaning: The scale of epic language makes the small social quarrel comically enormous.

title: Lyrical Ballads
author: William Wordsworth and S. T. Coleridge
setting: Ordinary lives, remembered landscapes and supernatural voyages
hook: An ordinary child, a haunted sailor, and a remembered landscape open new doors for poetry.

characters.name: Wordsworth
characters.role: Poet of ordinary life and memory

scenes.title: A new poetic direction
scenes.text: In 1798, Wordsworth and Coleridge brought out poems that looked beyond grand heroes. Country people, familiar feelings, and strange adventures could all deserve a reader's attention.

scenes.title: The ordinary life becomes worth a poem
scenes.text: A rural life could carry as much emotional weight as a royal one. The collection asks us to pause beside people whom fashionable poetry might pass by.
scenes.cue: THE ORDINARY LIFE BECOMES WORTH A POEM

scenes.title: Seven children or five
scenes.text: In We Are Seven, an adult meets a girl who counts two dead siblings among her family. He insists that only five remain. She keeps answering seven.

scenes.title: A child's answer resists adult counting
scenes.text: The girl visits the graves and still feels connected to those children. The adult counts living bodies; she counts belonging. Neither answer persuades the other.
scenes.cue: A CHILD'S ANSWER RESISTS ADULT COUNTING

scenes.title: The albatross is killed
scenes.text: In The Rime of the Ancient Mariner, a sailor kills an albatross that had accompanied his ship. The voyage darkens, and an apparently small act acquires terrible consequences.

scenes.title: The strange voyage asks for belief
scenes.text: Impossible events surround that sailor, but his fear and loneliness remain recognisable. The supernatural journey gives ordinary feelings a strange and unforgettable setting.
scenes.cue: THE STRANGE VOYAGE ASKS FOR BELIEF

scenes.title: Blessing living things
scenes.text: When the Mariner blesses living creatures without thinking of himself, the burden begins to loosen. His changed attention offers release, though it does not erase his experience.

scenes.title: Memory changes a returning landscape
scenes.text: Elsewhere, a speaker returns to the landscape near Tintern Abbey. Years away have changed him. The familiar river now holds both what he sees and what he remembers.

scenes.title: Guilt does not vanish with release
scenes.text: The Mariner must continue telling his story. Survival does not end his guilt, and a listener inherits his warning. One poem's release remains unlike another's quiet return.

scenes.title: Return to Tintern Abbey
scenes.text: At Tintern Abbey, memory becomes a companion through absence and change. The speaker shares his hopes with his sister, imagining that this place may comfort her too.

scenes.title: The preface follows the experiment
scenes.text: Wordsworth later added a preface explaining the experiment. He defended ordinary language and everyday experience as material for poetry. The explanation followed the poems that had tested those ideas.

scenes.title: The poems work differently
scenes.text: The collection is a doorway into several different voices, not one continuous adventure. Carry its child, sailor, and returning walker together: each changes what a reader notices.

question: How do the two poets' approaches differ?
answer: Wordsworth often renews everyday experience; Coleridge gives supernatural events emotional credibility.
note: Collection overview and representative poems, not a single invented storyline.

quotes.text: emotion recollected in tranquillity
quotes.context: Wordsworth's Preface, added in 1800 and expanded in 1802.
quotes.meaning: Feeling becomes poetry through later reflection, linking experience with the remembering mind.

title: The Excursion
author: William Wordsworth
setting: A rural landscape in England
hook: Travellers stop at a ruined cottage, and a quiet landscape begins to disclose human loss.

scenes.title: The journey begins
scenes.text: On a walk through the countryside, a poet meets the Wanderer, an experienced former travelling salesman. Their journey becomes a series of conversations about suffering, belief, and hope.

scenes.title: The walker carries another life
scenes.text: The Wanderer has listened to many people over a long working life. His reflections carry those encounters. When he speaks of hardship, individual lives stand behind the words.

scenes.title: The cottage keeps a human history
scenes.text: They stop at a ruined cottage. Its abandoned surroundings seem quiet, but the Wanderer remembers who lived there. The building has a story the passing traveller cannot see.

scenes.title: The abandoned cottage holds a story
scenes.text: He recalls Margaret, whose household once occupied the cottage. What remains outside gives little hint of her prolonged suffering. Listening turns an empty place into a human history.
scenes.cue: THE ABANDONED COTTAGE HOLDS A STORY

scenes.title: Margaret's story
scenes.text: Poverty, her husband's departure, and loss wore Margaret down. She waited and suffered until she died. The cottage's ruin becomes the visible ending of that slow disappearance.

scenes.title: The recluse has reasons for despair
scenes.text: The travellers also meet the Solitary, a man withdrawn after bereavement and disappointed political hopes. His despair has a history. Cheerful reassurance cannot simply remove it.
scenes.cue: THE RECLUSE HAS REASONS FOR DESPAIR

scenes.title: The Solitary's despair
scenes.text: The Solitary questions beliefs that once offered comfort. The Wanderer answers, but their discussion remains difficult. Another person's sorrow cannot be settled by winning an argument.

scenes.title: The exchange cannot be won by a slogan
scenes.text: Their talk circles through nature, faith, memory, and community. Hope has to meet the objections grief raises. It grows slowly within conversation rather than arriving as an instant cure.
scenes.cue: THE EXCHANGE CANNOT BE WON BY A SLOGAN

scenes.title: The answer is not only argument
scenes.text: The movement toward other people matters as much as the exchange of ideas. A lonely life may need companionship and shared duties alongside explanations of the world.

scenes.title: Lives in the churchyard
scenes.text: A Pastor leads them through accounts of people buried in a churchyard. Each grave opens another life. The debate now encounters names, choices, and losses within a community.

scenes.title: The local dead extend the argument
scenes.text: These remembered neighbours give the speakers something concrete to consider. General claims about suffering meet the varied lives of actual people, whose stories resist one easy conclusion.
scenes.cue: THE LOCAL DEAD EXTEND THE ARGUMENT

scenes.title: Hope remains a discussion
scenes.text: The poem leaves hope as something discussed and practised together. Remember the walk from cottage to churchyard: places grow fuller when someone stops to tell who lived there.

question: What is the main narrative method?
answer: Walking, conversation and remembered lives, through which the speakers debate suffering and hope.

quotes.text: We live by Admiration, Hope, and Love;
quotes.context: The Wanderer, Book IV.
quotes.meaning: These sustaining attachments answer the Solitary's despair without erasing the suffering behind it.

title: Frankenstein
author: Mary Shelley
setting: Geneva, the Alps and the Arctic
hook: A scientist creates life, runs from it, and discovers that abandonment has consequences.

characters.name: Justine
characters.role: Woman wrongly blamed for William’s death

scenes.title: An Arctic warning
scenes.text: Among Arctic ice, explorer Robert Walton rescues an exhausted stranger. Victor Frankenstein begins a warning about the ambition that brought him there. Walton, hungry for discovery, is ready to listen.

scenes.title: The listener also wants greatness
scenes.text: Walton dreams of achieving something extraordinary. Victor recognises that hunger. Before describing his experiment, he places its story before a man who might follow a similar road.

scenes.title: Life abandoned
scenes.text: Victor recalls creating a living being through scientific study. When it opens its eyes, he is horrified and flees. His achievement begins with a frightened creature left alone.

scenes.title: The maker flees the first need
scenes.text: The creature must learn without the maker's care. Hunger, cold, and people's fear become his first teachers. Victor has brought life into the world but refuses its first needs.
scenes.cue: THE MAKER FLEES THE FIRST NEED

scenes.title: The family behind the wall
scenes.text: Hidden beside the De Lacey family's cottage, the creature learns language and watches affection. He secretly helps them. Their household gives him a hope: perhaps he could belong somewhere.
scenes.cue: LEARNING opens a need for belonging

scenes.title: The hoped-for welcome ends in rejection
scenes.text: He approaches the blind father, hoping to be heard before being judged by appearance. The others return and reject him. The home he imagined entering becomes another closed door.
scenes.cue: THE HOPED-FOR WELCOME ENDS IN REJECTION

scenes.title: Rejection turns violent
scenes.text: Isolation hardens into anger. The creature turns from seeking welcome toward revenge against the man who abandoned him. Victor's private experiment begins harming the people around its maker.

scenes.title: A child becomes another victim
scenes.text: The creature kills Victor's young brother William and frames Justine. She is executed. Victor knows his creation is involved, but his silence cannot save the innocent woman.

scenes.title: A companion is negotiated
scenes.text: Meeting Victor in the mountains, the creature tells his own story and demands a companion. Someone like himself, he argues, could end the loneliness driving his violence.

scenes.title: Two lives are imagined beyond society
scenes.text: He promises that the pair would leave human society. Victor agrees, then fears what another creation might do. A possible refuge and a possible future danger become inseparable.
scenes.cue: TWO LIVES ARE IMAGINED BEYOND SOCIETY

scenes.title: The promise is broken
scenes.text: Victor destroys the unfinished companion. The creature retaliates, killing Clerval and later Victor's bride Elizabeth. Trying to avoid one feared consequence, Victor brings revenge back into his family.

scenes.title: Pursuit into ice
scenes.text: Victor pursues the creature into the ice and dies aboard Walton's ship. The creature mourns, then departs with a promise to end his own life. Walton turns his endangered crew toward home.

question: Who is Frankenstein?
answer: Victor, the creator. His creature is not given a personal name.
note: Summary based on the 1818 text. The ending reports the creature's intention; his death is not witnessed.

quotes.text: I ought to be thy Adam
quotes.context: The creature confronting Victor, Chapter 10 in the 1831 edition.
quotes.meaning: The abandoned creation asks his maker to recognise responsibility and the need for belonging.

title: Vanity Fair
author: William Makepeace Thackeray
setting: Britain and Europe around the Napoleonic wars
hook: Two school friends enter a world where money changes which ambitions people forgive.

scenes.title: Two friends leave school
scenes.text: Becky Sharp and Amelia Sedley leave school for very different futures. Amelia has a comfortable family; Becky has intelligence and few resources. Both enter a society absorbed in status.

scenes.title: The school gate opens onto unequal futures
scenes.text: Their friendship cannot give Becky Amelia's advantages. One woman can initially expect security; the other must find a way into wealthy households. The same social doors open differently.
scenes.cue: THE SCHOOL GATE OPENS ONTO UNEQUAL FUTURES

scenes.title: The inherited fortune redirects affection
scenes.text: Money redirects the people around them. A family's rise or fall can alter friendships and marriage prospects. Affection is constantly tested by the fortune attached to its object.

scenes.title: Charm learns to travel upward
scenes.text: Becky learns to charm people who can help her advance. Her performance is clever, but the world judging her also rewards that performance. She studies its rules closely.

scenes.title: Two marriages
scenes.text: Amelia marries George Osborne; Becky marries Rawdon Crawley. Neither wedding ends the contest for money and standing. The husbands bring weaknesses of their own into the marriages.

scenes.title: The wedding does not settle devotion
scenes.text: Amelia idealises George, though his attention wanders. Her devotion does not make him trustworthy. The picture she treasures already leaves uncomfortable facts outside its frame.
scenes.cue: THE WEDDING DOES NOT SETTLE DEVOTION

scenes.title: Waterloo divides their lives
scenes.text: The threat of war interrupts parties and private manoeuvres. The characters travel toward the world of Waterloo, where a social disappointment can suddenly become a permanent loss.

scenes.title: War interrupts the marriage market
scenes.text: George is killed in battle. Amelia becomes a widow, holding their child and her memory of him. The marriage's unresolved problems are now hidden beneath grief.

scenes.title: A widow keeps an ideal image
scenes.text: She continues loving an ideal George. Dobbin, who has long cared for her, waits nearby. His patient devotion cannot reach her while that remembered husband fills the future.

scenes.title: Society's glitter cracks
scenes.text: Becky's pursuit of glamour brings scandal and separation from Rawdon. Her success proves unstable. The polished rooms of fashionable life cannot keep their private bargains concealed forever.

scenes.title: A patient lover needs honest recognition
scenes.text: Dobbin finally resists being taken for granted. Amelia must see both his value and the truth about George. Recognition requires letting go of the story she preferred.
scenes.cue: A PATIENT LOVER NEEDS HONEST RECOGNITION

scenes.title: Loyalty finally recognised
scenes.text: Amelia and Dobbin eventually marry; Becky keeps manoeuvring through life. The fair of vanity continues around them. Remember how easily affection becomes confused with the image one wants to love.

question: What does the title's fair suggest?
answer: A marketplace in which people trade money, marriage, reputation and status.

quotes.text: Which of us is happy in this world?
quotes.context: Narrator, the novel's closing paragraph.
quotes.meaning: The final question tests whether winning status or desire has actually brought satisfaction.

title: In Memoriam A.H.H.
author: Alfred, Lord Tennyson
setting: Memory, changing seasons and landscapes of grief
hook: A friend's death changes the sound of Christmas bells and the meaning of a familiar world.

characters.name: Arthur Henry Hallam
characters.role: Lost friend and subject of the elegy

scenes.title: The absent friend
scenes.text: When Arthur Hallam died, Tennyson lost a close friend and the future they might have shared. This sequence of poems begins inside that absence, returning to it again and again.

scenes.title: The name carries a missing voice
scenes.text: Hallam remains present through memory, but cannot answer. The speaker addresses a friendship that has changed its form. Words keep reaching toward someone beyond their reply.
scenes.cue: THE NAME CARRIES A MISSING VOICE

scenes.title: The individual is not replaceable
scenes.text: No general comfort can replace this particular person. Other lives continue around the speaker, yet the loss is not interchangeable. Grief holds tightly to a face and a voice.

scenes.title: Words cannot equal the loss
scenes.text: The speaker doubts whether poetry can express sorrow faithfully. Language may seem too small or too polished. Still, writing becomes a way to remain with the difficult feeling.

scenes.title: Seasons return
scenes.text: Seasons pass, and familiar occasions return. Outward time moves forward while memory circles back. The changing year does not ask permission before carrying the bereaved person with it.

scenes.title: Another Christmas arrives without him
scenes.text: Christmas comes again without Hallam. Bells and household customs recall earlier happiness, but now sound against an empty place. The ordinary calendar becomes a measure of loss.

scenes.title: Nature unsettles faith
scenes.text: Nature itself troubles the speaker's faith. If living things struggle and perish without protection, what does that say about divine care? The world offers unsettling evidence.

scenes.title: Nature gives an unsettling answer
scenes.text: The question grows larger than one bereavement. A whole understanding of creation seems threatened by suffering. The speaker cannot recover belief merely by refusing to look.

scenes.title: Doubt does not end the search
scenes.text: Doubt recurs, but so does the desire for meaning. The poems allow those movements to coexist. A hopeful moment does not cancel every question raised before it.

scenes.title: Love survives uncertainty
scenes.text: Love for Hallam survives even where certainty falters. The speaker gradually imagines an attachment continuing beyond physical presence. Consolation arrives in uneven steps rather than one decisive revelation.

scenes.title: The attachment becomes an inward influence
scenes.text: Hallam's remembered character begins to influence the life still being lived. The missing friend becomes an inward companion, shaping the speaker's hopes and moral imagination.
scenes.cue: THE ATTACHMENT BECOMES AN INWARD INFLUENCE

scenes.title: A wedding opens the future
scenes.text: A wedding finally opens the sequence toward another generation. Mourning has not erased Hallam, but life can move toward a future. The empty place remains within a larger love.

question: Is the poem a straight sequence from sadness to happiness?
answer: No. Grief, doubt and hope recur across its lyrics; the journey is not a simple linear cure.
note: Published before Darwin's On the Origin of Species in 1859. These frames are thematic landmarks rather than a continuous plot.

quotes.text: 'Tis better to have loved and lost
quotes.context: Section 27; the thought is completed by the following line.
quotes.meaning: The speaker values attachment despite grief; this conviction emerges within a long struggle with doubt.

title: The Return of the Native
author: Thomas Hardy
setting: Egdon Heath in Wessex
hook: On a dark heath, one person dreams of escape while another comes home to stay.

scenes.title: Two opposite dreams
scenes.text: On Egdon Heath, Eustacia Vye longs for a more exciting life. Clym Yeobright returns from Paris, hoping to educate his neighbours. Their dreams move in opposite directions.

scenes.title: The heath keeps its own rhythm
scenes.text: The heath surrounds them with an older, slower life. Its paths and weather will outlast each quarrel. Human desire burns brightly against a landscape that does not hurry.
scenes.cue: THE HEATH KEEPS ITS OWN RHYTHM

scenes.title: The bonfires bring distant watchers together
scenes.text: Bonfires draw people onto the dark heath. From a distance, watchers see signals and imagine possibilities. Eustacia's wish to leave begins linking her to other people's unsettled relationships.

scenes.title: Escape and return point opposite ways
scenes.text: To Eustacia, Clym might be a doorway to Paris. To Clym, returning home is the purpose. Each sees a future in the other that the other has not promised.
scenes.cue: ESCAPE AND RETURN POINT OPPOSITE WAYS

scenes.title: An unstable triangle
scenes.text: Damon Wildeve, once drawn to Eustacia, marries Thomasin. Attraction does not settle neatly into the new arrangement. Past desires keep crossing the paths of the newly married.

scenes.title: Marriage without a shared future
scenes.text: Eustacia marries Clym, but the life she expects fails to arrive. He remains committed to the heath. Love has brought them together without giving them a shared direction.

scenes.title: The wished-for teacher faces a different life
scenes.text: Clym's eyesight fails, interrupting his educational plans. He takes practical work cutting furze. Eustacia sees the hoped-for escape receding while her husband struggles with changed circumstances.
scenes.cue: THE WISHED-FOR TEACHER FACES A DIFFERENT LIFE

scenes.title: Money changes the imagined escape
scenes.text: Wildeve gains money, making another escape seem possible. His renewed contact with Eustacia complicates the marriage further. A different future glimmers precisely when her present life disappoints her.

scenes.title: The unopened door
scenes.text: Clym's mother visits their house but leaves believing she has been rejected. Exhausted on the heath, she later dies. A closed door becomes the centre of a terrible misunderstanding.

scenes.title: The closed door grows into a tragedy
scenes.text: Clym learns what happened and blames Eustacia. What each person knew at the doorway was different, but the consequences gather inside their marriage. Reconciliation becomes harder.
scenes.cue: THE CLOSED DOOR GROWS INTO A TRAGEDY

scenes.title: The final journey does not explain itself
scenes.text: During a storm, Eustacia sets out toward a possible escape and drowns. The account leaves her intention uncertain. Neither a confident accident story nor a confident suicide story settles it.
scenes.cue: THE FINAL JOURNEY DOES NOT EXPLAIN ITSELF

scenes.title: Storm at the weir
scenes.text: Wildeve also dies in the water; others survive to rebuild altered lives. Clym turns toward preaching, while Thomasin later finds another marriage. The heath remains around their losses.

question: What makes Clym and Eustacia's marriage unstable?
answer: He wants a meaningful life on the heath; she imagines him taking her away from it.
note: Clym plans to teach but eyesight problems prevent the project. Eustacia's death remains ambiguous rather than an established suicide.

quotes.text: Egdon was aroused to reciprocity
quotes.context: Book I, Chapter 1, twilight on the heath.
quotes.meaning: The setting seems to answer the darkening sky, making the heath an active presence around human lives.

title: A Doll’s House
author: Henrik Ibsen
setting: The Helmer home in Norway
hook: A cheerful Christmas household contains a debt the husband knows nothing about.

scenes.title: Christmas and appearances
scenes.text: Christmas arrives in Nora and Torvald Helmer's comfortable home. He looks forward to a better salary; she buys presents. Beneath the cheerful preparations, Nora guards a secret.

scenes.title: The pet names define a role
scenes.text: Torvald calls her affectionate little names and treats her like a dependent child. The warmth comes with control. He does not imagine her as someone making serious decisions.
scenes.cue: THE PET NAMES DEFINE A ROLE

scenes.title: The apparently childish woman has worked
scenes.text: Yet Nora has quietly worked and saved to repay borrowed money. The apparently carefree wife has carried a hidden burden. Every small payment helps keep her secret out of view.

scenes.title: The borrowed money paid for care
scenes.text: The loan paid for travel that helped save Torvald's life. Nora acted because she loved him. But obtaining the money required a signature she did not have authority to use.
scenes.cue: THE BORROWED MONEY PAID FOR CARE

scenes.title: The secret loan
scenes.text: She forged her father's signature. Now the lender, Krogstad, threatens to reveal it. The act Nora remembers as care has become a legal danger hanging over her marriage.

scenes.title: A threatened job becomes leverage
scenes.text: Krogstad may lose his bank position under Torvald. He uses the secret to press Nora for help. Her husband's decision about a job could expose the wife he thinks he understands.

scenes.title: Dancing against time
scenes.text: At a party, Nora dances the tarantella while a revealing letter waits at home. Her movement looks festive. Behind it, she is desperately trying to delay Torvald's discovery.

scenes.title: The dance tries to hold back time
scenes.text: She keeps his attention on the dance, hoping to hold back time. The letter remains in the box. When the music ends, the household's carefully maintained appearance will still face it.
scenes.cue: THE DANCE TRIES TO HOLD BACK TIME

scenes.title: Kristine chooses a truth that must be heard
scenes.text: Nora's friend Kristine decides the couple must confront the truth. A renewed understanding with Krogstad could stop the threat, but concealment would leave the marriage's deeper problem untouched.
scenes.cue: HONESTY is not always comfortable protection

scenes.title: The husband's response
scenes.text: Torvald reads the letter and attacks Nora for endangering his reputation. He does not first thank her for saving his life. His response breaks the rescue she had imagined.

scenes.title: The expected rescue does not arrive
scenes.text: When the danger passes, Torvald offers forgiveness and expects their old life to resume. Nora has heard something she cannot unhear. Safety has returned; her belief in the marriage has not.
scenes.cue: THE EXPECTED RESCUE DOES NOT ARRIVE

scenes.title: The door closes
scenes.text: She decides to leave and educate herself beyond the role of doll wife. Torvald cannot persuade her to stay. The closing door makes her new, uncertain life audible.

question: What destroys Nora's belief in her marriage?
answer: Torvald's response to the letter reveals that he prioritises reputation over understanding her sacrifice.
note: The play does not establish that Nora's departure is temporary.

quotes.text: I have been your doll-wife
quotes.context: Nora to Torvald, Act III; R. Farquharson Sharp translation.
quotes.meaning: Nora names the performance of dependence that has shaped their marriage.

title: Tess of the d’Urbervilles
author: Thomas Hardy
setting: Rural Wessex
hook: An old family name promises rescue, but sends a young woman toward danger.

scenes.title: A name promises fortune
scenes.text: In a poor rural household, Tess's father learns that his family descends from the old d'Urbervilles. The impressive name seems to promise a way out of hardship.

scenes.title: An old name promises a false road
scenes.text: The family seeks help from wealthy people using that name. Their hoped-for connection is misleading. Tess is sent toward a household whose apparent kinship offers no real protection.
scenes.cue: AN OLD NAME PROMISES A FALSE ROAD

scenes.title: The horse dies and responsibility presses
scenes.text: After the family's horse dies, Tess feels responsible for their worsening position. That pressure helps send her to work near Alec d'Urberville. Need narrows the choices she can make.

scenes.title: The harmed woman carries the judgement
scenes.text: Alec sexually harms Tess. Afterwards, her community places shame upon her rather than protection around her. The young woman must carry social punishment for harm done to her.
scenes.cue: THE HARMED WOMAN CARRIES THE JUDGEMENT

scenes.title: Harm and loss
scenes.text: She returns home and bears a child. The name that was meant to improve her future has led to suffering. She tries to go on in a world quick to judge.

scenes.title: The child's life is painfully brief
scenes.text: Her baby becomes ill and dies. Tess's private grief meets religious and social restrictions even at burial. The child's brief life leaves another wound she must carry forward.
scenes.cue: THE CHILD'S LIFE IS PAINFULLY BRIEF

scenes.title: A dairy and a new hope
scenes.text: At a dairy, Tess meets Angel Clare and begins to hope again. Work, affection, and a different landscape offer a new beginning. But her unspoken history follows her there.

scenes.title: The warning does not reach its reader
scenes.text: She writes a confession before their marriage, but Angel does not read it. Her attempt at honesty fails through circumstance. They enter the wedding with unequal knowledge.
scenes.cue: A MESSAGE unseen cannot create understanding

scenes.title: The double standard
scenes.text: On their wedding night, both confess a past sexual experience. Tess forgives Angel. He refuses to offer the same forgiveness to her, and the marriage breaks apart.

scenes.title: Two confessions receive unequal answers
scenes.text: Angel leaves, holding Tess to a standard he does not apply to himself. She works under harsh conditions while trying to survive. The hoped-for refuge has become another abandonment.

scenes.title: The hoped-for return arrives too late
scenes.text: Alec returns, and family poverty draws Tess back under his power. When Angel finally recognises his wrong and comes back, he finds a life changed by his absence.
scenes.cue: THE HOPED-FOR RETURN ARRIVES TOO LATE

scenes.title: Too late for rescue
scenes.text: Tess kills Alec, briefly escapes with Angel, and is arrested at Stonehenge. She is executed. Angel's return brought recognition, but came too late to undo the consequences.

question: What is Angel's double standard?
answer: He expects forgiveness for his sexual past while refusing to accept Tess's history of exploitation.
note: The encounter with Alec is narrated elliptically; this adaptation avoids presenting Tess as responsible for her exploitation.

quotes.text: “Justice” was done
quotes.context: Narrator, Chapter 59.
