scenes.text: Wordsworth turns toward childhood to tell how a poet's mind grew. The adventure is not a single quest. It follows experiences that continued shaping him after they were over.
scenes.cue: THE SUBJECT is a growing mind

scenes.title: The growing mind becomes the subject
scenes.text: Ordinary days become part of that growth. Feeling, memory, and attention gradually make a vocation. The young person does not yet know which moments will prove important.
scenes.cue: THE GROWING MIND BECOMES THE SUBJECT

scenes.title: The stolen boat
scenes.text: As a boy, he takes a boat without permission and rows onto a lake. Pleasure changes when a dark peak seems to rise behind him. The scene feels suddenly immense.

scenes.title: The stolen boat brings an unexpected watcher
scenes.text: The mountain appears to pursue the moving boat. Fear follows him after he returns it. A youthful act leaves an image larger than the moment that produced it.
scenes.cue: THE STOLEN BOAT BRINGS AN UNEXPECTED WATCHER

scenes.title: Learning among landscapes
scenes.text: Hills, lakes, and solitary wandering teach him through delight and unease. Nature is not always gentle. Its power helps enlarge the imagination that will later remember it.

scenes.title: Skating makes movement a kind of learning
scenes.text: Skating with other children gives him speed, sound, and the changing feel of space. When movement stops, the world seems to continue. Bodily experience becomes lasting wonder.
scenes.cue: SKATING MAKES MOVEMENT A KIND OF LEARNING

scenes.title: Books and crowded life
scenes.text: Books and education open other worlds. The growing mind learns from human invention as well as landscape. Its development crosses between reading, experience, and inward response.

scenes.title: The city offers another crowd of impressions
scenes.text: London surrounds him with crowds, spectacle, and unfamiliar encounters. The city strains and stimulates his attention. Its multitude offers another kind of landscape to interpret.
scenes.cue: THE CITY OFFERS ANOTHER CROWD OF IMPRESSIONS

scenes.title: Revolution promises renewal
scenes.text: The French Revolution initially seems to promise human renewal. He invests hope in political change. The imagination that found meaning in nature now reaches toward history.

scenes.title: Disillusion and recovery
scenes.text: Violence and disappointment unsettle those hopes. His confidence breaks, and recovery requires time, affection, and renewed attention. Political disillusion does not leave the inward life untouched.

scenes.title: A remembered moment can still repair
scenes.text: Remembered moments, later called spots of time, retain a power to restore him. An earlier experience can keep working after its occasion ends. Memory becomes more than storage.
scenes.cue: A REMEMBERED MOMENT CAN STILL REPAIR

scenes.title: A vocation takes shape
scenes.text: The poem gathers these experiences into the making of a poet. Keep the boy on the lake beside the adult remembering him: imagination grows partly by returning to what it once feared.

question: Why is the boat-stealing episode important?
answer: Fear transforms an ordinary excursion into an experience that continues to shape the child's imagination.
note: Published posthumously in 1850, with earlier major versions in 1799 and 1805. Placed with Romantic works by movement despite its Victorian publication date.

quotes.text: spots of time
quotes.context: Book XII of the 1850 text.
quotes.meaning: Certain remembered experiences retain a power to restore the mind long after the original event.

title: The Rime of the Ancient Mariner
author: S. T. Coleridge
setting: A wedding frame and a haunted sea voyage
hook: A wedding guest is stopped by a sailor whose story begins with an unexplained killing.

scenes.title: The wedding interrupted
scenes.text: On the way to a wedding, a guest is stopped by an old sailor. The Mariner fixes him with a compelling gaze. Celebration continues nearby while a darker voyage begins in words.

scenes.title: The listener wants the wedding instead
scenes.text: The guest wants to join the feast, but cannot leave the tale. He becomes its unwilling listener. The Mariner's need to speak takes precedence over the day's festivities.
scenes.cue: THE LISTENER WANTS THE WEDDING INSTEAD

scenes.title: The bird follows the ship
scenes.text: The sailor recalls a ship driven into ice. An albatross appeared and accompanied them as the weather improved. The crew welcomed the bird as a helpful presence.

scenes.title: The killing has no satisfying explanation
scenes.text: Then the Mariner shot it. The poem gives no satisfying motive that would make the act reasonable. A sudden injury to a living creature changes the voyage.
scenes.cue: THE KILLING HAS NO SATISFYING EXPLANATION

scenes.title: A still and thirsty sea
scenes.text: The ship reaches a still, scorching sea. Water surrounds the sailors, yet none is drinkable. The crew hangs the dead albatross around the Mariner's neck as a burden of blame.

scenes.title: The water cannot answer thirst
scenes.text: Thirst silences them. The familiar sea becomes an impossible prison, holding plenty of water and no relief. Movement, speech, and hope seem to dry up together.

scenes.title: The spectral game
scenes.text: A spectral ship approaches. Death and Life-in-Death gamble for the sailors; the Mariner survives while his companions die. Winning life becomes its own terrible sentence.

scenes.title: Survival becomes the heavier sentence
scenes.text: Alone among the bodies, he cannot pray or escape their gaze. Survival offers no companionship. The killing has left him with a world he struggles to love.

scenes.title: An unplanned blessing
scenes.text: Watching water snakes, he suddenly recognises their beauty and blesses them. The feeling comes without a plan for reward. His attention changes before he understands its consequence.

scenes.title: The blessing arrives before calculation
scenes.text: The albatross falls from his neck, and prayer becomes possible. Relief begins through an uncalculated regard for living things. The voyage's punishment has not yet fully ended.

scenes.title: The return and the confession
scenes.text: He eventually returns home, but a recurring agony drives him to tell his story. He teaches reverence for living creatures. Confession becomes the work his survival requires.

scenes.title: A sadder wiser listener
scenes.text: The wedding guest leaves changed and misses the celebration. The tale has interrupted more than his route to a feast. He wakes with a sadder, deeper understanding.

question: What releases the albatross from the Mariner's neck?
answer: His spontaneous blessing of the water snakes, a moment of uncalculated love for living things.
note: First version appeared in Lyrical Ballads. This individual entry expands the poem only briefly introduced in the collection.

quotes.text: He prayeth best, who loveth best
quotes.context: Part VII, the Mariner's concluding lesson.
quotes.meaning: The voyage's guilt and recovery lead toward care for living beings beyond the self.

title: Kubla Khan
author: S. T. Coleridge
setting: Xanadu and a remembered imaginative vision
hook: A ruler encloses a pleasure garden, while an untamed river carries the vision beyond his walls.

characters.name: The Abyssinian maid
characters.role: Figure whose music the speaker remembers

scenes.title: The dome is decreed
scenes.text: Imagine Xanadu, where Kubla Khan commands a magnificent pleasure dome. Gardens and walls promise controlled beauty. Through the scene runs Alph, a river leading toward a sunless sea.

scenes.title: The imperial command draws a boundary
scenes.text: The ruler marks out an ordered enclosure. His command can arrange gardens, but the poem's wider landscape will not stay within that plan. Other forces are already moving beneath it.
scenes.cue: THE IMPERIAL COMMAND DRAWS A BOUNDARY

scenes.title: The river travels beyond order
scenes.text: The river passes through caverns beyond human measure. Its course exceeds the boundaries of the pleasure ground. The vision joins carefully cultivated space to something immense and unknown.

scenes.title: The river ignores the enclosure’s promise
scenes.text: Water moves from the visible garden into hidden depths. What can be enclosed is only part of the world. The ruler's splendid decree cannot explain the whole journey.
scenes.cue: THE RIVER IGNORES THE ENCLOSURE’S PROMISE

scenes.title: The chasm erupts
scenes.text: A deep chasm breaks the landscape, associated with wildness and supernatural disturbance. The peaceful garden now has a restless neighbour. Its beauty depends on a contrast it cannot remove.

scenes.title: The fountain brings power from below
scenes.text: A fountain erupts from that chasm, throwing rocks upward. The river's energy rises violently from below. Creation appears as both an ordered design and an uncontrollable force.
scenes.cue: THE FOUNTAIN BRINGS POWER FROM BELOW

scenes.title: The ancestors warn
scenes.text: Kubla hears ancestral voices prophesying war. Danger enters the splendid scene before the vision ends. The pleasure dome cannot make its own future permanently peaceful.

scenes.title: The shadow contains an impossible contrast
scenes.text: Its shadow lies across the water, joining a sunny dome to caves of ice. The impossible contrast feels convincing inside the vision. Ordinary rules no longer control the picture.
scenes.cue: THE SHADOW CONTAINS AN IMPOSSIBLE CONTRAST

scenes.title: Music returns in memory
scenes.text: The speaker remembers a maiden playing a dulcimer and singing of Mount Abora. Another image enters, now through music. The remembered song might restore the creative power he seeks.

scenes.title: The wished-for reconstruction
scenes.text: He wishes he could recover that song completely. With its music, he imagines building the dome in air. The ruler's visible construction becomes the poet's hoped-for imaginative creation.

scenes.title: The remembered song might rebuild the dome
scenes.text: The desired song is not shown returning in full. The speaker imagines what its recovery would make possible. The gap between remembered beauty and present ability remains.
scenes.cue: THE REMEMBERED SONG MIGHT REBUILD THE DOME

scenes.title: The poet becomes uncanny
scenes.text: The inspired poet appears both wonderful and frightening, someone listeners would approach with awe. The fragment ends around that imagined power, leaving its enchanted architecture suspended.

question: What changes when the Abyssinian maid appears?
answer: The focus shifts from Kubla's commanded palace to the speaker's wish to recover a musical vision and create through poetry.
note: Published 1816. Coleridge's preface describes a dream and an interruption; these are part of his account, not independently verified facts.

quotes.text: A sunny pleasure-dome with caves of ice!
quotes.context: The visionary contrast near the end of the landscape description.
quotes.meaning: Opposite images make the imagined creation dazzling, unstable and difficult to recover.

title: Ozymandias
author: Percy Bysshe Shelley
setting: An ancient ruin in a desert
hook: A broken statue still commands admiration, in a desert that has forgotten its kingdom.

characters.name: Ozymandias
characters.role: King represented by a broken statue

scenes.title: A report from afar
scenes.text: A speaker meets a traveller from an ancient land. The traveller describes a ruined statue in the desert. A long-dead ruler reaches us through someone else's report.

scenes.title: The ruler reaches us through a stranger
scenes.text: There is no direct audience with this king. His authority passes through broken stone and a traveller's words. Time has changed who gets to describe him.
scenes.cue: THE RULER REACHES US THROUGH A STRANGER

scenes.title: The body is broken
scenes.text: Two huge legs stand without a body. Nearby lies a shattered face. The scale suggests former magnificence, while the damage shows how little that magnificence could protect.

scenes.title: The fallen face still knows how to command
scenes.text: The fallen face still wears a sneer and commanding expression. Power survives as an image after losing its living instrument. The ruler can look imperious but issue no effective order.
scenes.cue: THE FALLEN FACE STILL KNOWS HOW TO COMMAND

scenes.title: The expression survives
scenes.text: The sculptor understood the ruler's passions well enough to preserve them. The face records pride and cruelty. Another person's skill has kept this fragment of the king alive.

scenes.title: The artist’s hand has outlasted the throne
scenes.text: The artist's work outlasted the authority it represented. What remains belongs partly to the observer who carved it. The king's self-image is no longer entirely his own.
scenes.cue: THE ARTIST’S HAND HAS OUTLASTED THE THRONE

scenes.title: The pedestal speaks
scenes.text: An inscription names Ozymandias and boasts of his works. It orders mighty people to look and despair. For a moment, the ruined monument still speaks in the language of command.

scenes.title: The invitation asks for evidence nearby
scenes.text: That boast sends the listener searching for the promised achievements. The words expect visible proof nearby. Their confident invitation prepares the poem's sharpest turn.
scenes.cue: THE INVITATION ASKS FOR EVIDENCE NEARBY

scenes.title: The reader looks around
scenes.text: Nothing of the kingdom remains around the statue. The works that should inspire despair have vanished. The ruler's declaration now exposes the defeat it meant to deny.

scenes.title: The sands extend
scenes.text: Level sands extend into the distance. They make the enormous monument seem isolated and small. The landscape has no interest in preserving the scale of a king's ambition.

scenes.title: The desert gives no obedient answer
scenes.text: The desert does not answer the command with obedience. Its silence becomes the answer. A boast carved to last now measures how thoroughly power can disappear.
scenes.cue: THE DESERT GIVES NO OBEDIENT ANSWER

scenes.title: The irony completes the portrait
scenes.text: Remember the commanding face beside the empty sand. The poem's irony needs both images: pride survives in words, while the world those words claimed has gone.

question: Why is the inscription ironic?
answer: It demands admiration for lasting power while standing beside ruins surrounded by emptiness.
note: A progression through the sonnet's framed description, not an invented biography of the king.

quotes.text: Nothing beside remains.
quotes.context: The traveller's account, after the statue's boast.
quotes.meaning: The ruined setting overturns a ruler's claim to lasting power.

title: Ode to the West Wind
author: Percy Bysshe Shelley
setting: An autumn landscape and the speaker's imagination
hook: A poet watches a storm scatter dead leaves and asks it to carry his own words outward.

scenes.title: Leaves driven before the wind
scenes.text: An autumn wind drives dead leaves through the air. Shelley addresses it as a powerful presence. The season seems destructive, but its movement carries another possibility.

scenes.title: The dead leaves are not the whole story
scenes.text: The leaves are only the visible beginning. Seeds are travelling too, toward places where they will lie through winter. What looks like an ending also prepares future growth.
scenes.cue: THE DEAD LEAVES ARE NOT THE WHOLE STORY

scenes.title: Seeds await another season
scenes.text: The wind carries those seeds into waiting ground. Spring will awaken them later. The poem joins the scattering of what has died to the preservation of what may live.

scenes.title: The hidden seed waits within the season
scenes.text: For now, the seed stays hidden and still. Its future cannot be seen in the cold season. Renewal requires time beyond the storm's immediate spectacle.
scenes.cue: THE HIDDEN SEED WAITS WITHIN THE SEASON

scenes.title: The sky is transformed
scenes.text: The speaker looks upward as clouds move before the same force. The sky becomes another vast, rushing scene. The wind's power reaches beyond the leaves underfoot.

scenes.title: The clouds give the sky a rushing body
scenes.text: Storm clouds gather like a moving army. Their scale makes the coming rain feel immense. The year seems to approach its end beneath that darkening roof.
scenes.cue: THE CLOUDS GIVE THE SKY A RUSHING BODY

scenes.title: The sea responds
scenes.text: The sea responds too. Waters and imagined underwater growth feel the force. The invocation has moved through earth, sky, and water, giving the wind a world to touch.

scenes.title: The still sea is imagined waking
scenes.text: A calm sea is pictured awakening under its passage. Nothing in the speaker's vision stays entirely untouched. The restless power now seems capable of reaching his own life.
scenes.cue: THE STILL SEA IS IMAGINED WAKING

scenes.title: The speaker feels constrained
scenes.text: He feels burdened and confined, unlike the freer self he remembers. Watching the wind awakens a longing to move again. His request becomes personal.

scenes.title: Make the poet an instrument
scenes.text: He asks to become the wind's instrument, like a lyre sounding under its touch. Instead of commanding the force, he offers himself to its movement.

scenes.title: The poet wants to become the instrument
scenes.text: Let his words scatter like leaves and sparks, he asks, waking other minds. The storm becomes a model for poetic influence. A private burden reaches toward a public hope.
scenes.cue: THE POET WANTS TO BECOME THE INSTRUMENT

scenes.title: The question opens a future
scenes.text: The poem ends by asking whether spring can be far behind winter. Hope rises from the seasonal pattern. The ending promises possibility without pretending that the present cold has vanished.

question: Why is the wind both destroyer and preserver?
answer: It clears dead growth while carrying seeds that can germinate later.
note: Written 1819; published 1820. A five-section ode; seven frames unpack its imagery and turn toward the speaker.

quotes.text: If Winter comes, can Spring be far behind?
quotes.context: Canto V, final line.
quotes.meaning: The seasonal question converts destruction into the possibility of renewal.

title: Prometheus Unbound
author: Percy Bysshe Shelley
setting: A mythic landscape of oppression and release
hook: A chained rebel refuses to become like his tormentor, and a whole imagined world begins to change.

scenes.title: The suffering captive
scenes.text: Prometheus hangs bound under Jupiter's tyranny, suffering for helping humankind. The ruler can punish his body. The captive's refusal to yield keeps another kind of power alive.

scenes.title: The captive remembers his own hatred
scenes.text: Prometheus remembers the curse he once hurled at Jupiter. Hatred has tied his thoughts to the tyrant. To imagine liberation, he begins reconsidering that old response.
scenes.cue: THE CAPTIVE REMEMBERS HIS OWN HATRED

scenes.title: The curse is recalled
scenes.text: He asks to hear the curse again. Its violent words return from the past. Remembering makes him confront what his own rage had wished upon another being.

scenes.title: The recalled curse is answered by mercy
scenes.text: Now he withdraws the curse and rejects revenge. He will not make another's suffering his pleasure. The inward change begins before his physical chains are removed.
scenes.cue: THE RECALLED CURSE IS ANSWERED BY MERCY

scenes.title: Temptation and endurance
scenes.text: Jupiter sends terrifying pressures to break him. Prometheus endures without surrendering his new resolve. Resistance means refusing both submission and the tyrant's pattern of cruelty.

scenes.title: The torment reaches through fearful visions
scenes.text: The torment includes visions of human suffering. He cannot ignore the pain his struggle concerns. Compassion must survive the very images that make despair persuasive.
scenes.cue: THE TORMENT REACHES THROUGH FEARFUL VISIONS

scenes.title: Asia searches
scenes.text: His beloved Asia journeys with Panthea in search of the power behind change. Their movement carries the drama beyond the isolated captive. Liberation needs another path opening elsewhere.

scenes.title: The beloved’s journey searches for understanding
scenes.text: They seek understanding from Demogorgon. Questions about rule, destiny, and love lead toward Jupiter's fall. The imaginative journey connects personal endurance with a changed world order.
scenes.cue: THE BELOVED’S JOURNEY SEARCHES FOR UNDERSTANDING

scenes.title: Jupiter loses his throne
scenes.text: Demogorgon overthrows Jupiter. The authority that seemed eternal loses its throne. The poem refuses the assumption that tyranny must remain because it has long governed.

scenes.title: Release and reunion
scenes.text: Prometheus is released and reunited with Asia. His freedom answers more than a private wish. The drama imagines a wider liberation made possible by the collapse of oppression.

scenes.title: The changed world needs more than a new ruler
scenes.text: A changed world needs more than a replacement ruler. Love, imagination, and freedom must alter relationships themselves. Otherwise, another throne could repeat the old pattern.
scenes.cue: THE CHANGED WORLD NEEDS MORE THAN A NEW RULER

scenes.title: The imaginative world remade
scenes.text: The final vision celebrates renewal while preserving the demand for endurance and forgiveness. Remember the chained figure who abandoned revenge before release: freedom began in how he chose to resist.

question: Why does Prometheus withdraw his curse?
answer: He refuses to make hatred the foundation of the freedom he wants.
note: A four-act lyrical drama. The transformed world is a poetic vision, not a historical event.

quotes.text: To suffer woes which Hope thinks infinite;
quotes.context: Demogorgon's final speech, Act IV.
quotes.meaning: Resistance includes endurance and love rather than reproducing the tyrant's hatred.

title: Ode to a Nightingale
author: John Keats
setting: An imagined encounter with birdsong
hook: A bird's beautiful song makes a listener long to escape the world that hurts him.

characters.name: The speaker
characters.role: Drawn toward and away from mortality

scenes.title: Joy feels like an ache
scenes.text: A speaker hears a nightingale singing and feels an ache. The bird's apparent happiness unsettles him rather than simply cheering him. Beauty opens a longing he cannot immediately satisfy.

scenes.title: The beautiful song makes the listener ache
scenes.text: The pain comes from being intensely moved by another creature's song. He imagines its ease against his own human condition. The distance between them becomes the poem's journey.
scenes.cue: THE BEAUTIFUL SONG MAKES THE LISTENER ACHE

scenes.title: An imagined cup of escape
scenes.text: He first wishes for wine that could carry him away. Taste, warmth, and celebration fill the imagined cup. Escape begins as a desire to leave ordinary awareness behind.

scenes.title: The imagined drink promises distance
scenes.text: The drink promises a path from troubled life into the bird's world. It remains imagined rather than a journey actually taken. The longing changes shape as the poem continues.

scenes.title: The human world remembered
scenes.text: He recalls ageing, sickness, disappointment, and death. Human life loses beauty and love through time. The song seems to rise beyond conditions he cannot avoid.

scenes.title: The human world enters the comparison
scenes.text: That contrast deepens the wish to leave. The bird does not speak about those burdens. Its apparent freedom belongs partly to the speaker's imaginative view of it.
scenes.cue: THE HUMAN WORLD ENTERS THE COMPARISON

scenes.title: Poetry replaces the wine
scenes.text: He chooses poetry rather than wine as his vehicle. Imagination carries him toward the unseen singer. The movement occurs through language, without erasing the body that listens.

scenes.title: The darkness makes imagination more necessary
scenes.text: In darkness, he cannot see the flowers around him but imagines their scents and forms. Missing sight makes other sensations richer. The hidden world grows through attentive invention.
scenes.cue: THE DARKNESS MAKES IMAGINATION MORE NECESSARY

scenes.title: Death becomes tempting
scenes.text: He briefly imagines dying peacefully while the bird continues singing. Yet death would also end his hearing. The desired release contains the loss of the very beauty attracting him.

scenes.title: The song crosses history
scenes.text: He hears the song as something reaching through past generations and imagined distant lives. The bird's music seems older than any single listener. Its continuity contrasts with mortal lives.

scenes.title: The same song seems to cross centuries
scenes.text: Ancient figures and lonely travellers appear in that imaginative history. The song crosses distance without becoming a literal immortal bird. It is the recurring music that seems to endure.
scenes.cue: THE SAME SONG SEEMS TO CROSS CENTURIES

scenes.title: The music fades
scenes.text: The song fades, and the speaker returns to uncertainty. Was the experience vision or dream? The poem ends where imaginative escape meets the waking life still waiting.

question: In what sense is the bird imagined as immortal?
answer: Its recurring song seems to link listeners across time; the individual bird is not literally deathless.
note: First published 1819; included in the 1820 volume. The frames follow a lyric movement, not a physical expedition.

quotes.text: Was it a vision, or a waking dream?
quotes.context: Final stanza.
quotes.meaning: The speaker returns from imagined escape unable to settle the status of the experience.

title: To Autumn
author: John Keats
setting: Fields, orchards and an autumn evening
hook: A season gathers fruit, pauses beside the harvest, and finds music in its own ending.

scenes.title: Ripeness fills the scene
scenes.text: Picture a countryside full of ripe fruit and swelling crops. Keats addresses Autumn as a presence working beside the sun. The opening scene overflows with growth reaching fulfilment.

scenes.title: The season works with the sun
scenes.text: Branches bend and shells fill. Warmth and season cooperate in bringing things to maturity. Autumn begins here as abundance, not merely the approach of winter.
scenes.cue: THE SEASON WORKS WITH THE SUN

scenes.title: The bees think warmth will last
scenes.text: Late flowers keep the bees busy. With sweetness still available, the insects seem to think warm days will never finish. Their small activity carries the illusion of endless summer.

scenes.title: The bees mistake abundance for endlessness
scenes.text: The abundance feels so complete that an ending is difficult to imagine. Yet it belongs to a season already moving onward. Plenty and passing time occupy the same scene.
scenes.cue: THE BEES MISTAKE ABUNDANCE FOR ENDLESSNESS

scenes.title: The season rests
scenes.text: Autumn appears as a resting worker beside the harvest. The season receives a human posture. After growth's fullness comes a quieter interval of waiting and completion.

scenes.title: The resting figure gives time a body
scenes.text: Loose hair moves in a breeze; a half-reaped field pauses. The personified figure gives us something visible to hold. Time becomes a body lingering beside its work.
scenes.cue: THE RESTING FIGURE GIVES TIME A BODY

scenes.title: The harvest has its pauses
scenes.text: Other harvest images follow, including a gleaner and the cider press. Their activities proceed slowly. Ripeness has a rhythm different from spring's urgent beginning.

scenes.title: The cider press measures a patient ending
scenes.text: At the press, the last drops emerge patiently. The image makes completion gradual rather than abrupt. The season does not vanish all at once.
scenes.cue: THE CIDER PRESS MEASURES A PATIENT ENDING

scenes.title: Spring's song is not required
scenes.text: The speaker asks where spring's songs have gone, then finds no need to borrow them. Autumn has its own music. Its value does not depend on becoming another season.

scenes.title: Evening gathers its music
scenes.text: Evening fills with gnats, lambs, crickets, birds, and swallows. Sound gathers as daylight declines. The ending landscape is still inhabited and active.

scenes.title: The evening chorus belongs to this season
scenes.text: Each sound belongs to this moment of the year. The chorus offers life within change. An approaching winter does not silence the present scene beforehand.
scenes.cue: THE EVENING CHORUS BELONGS TO THIS SEASON

scenes.title: The ending holds movement
scenes.text: Hold the poem's movement from ripeness through harvest to evening music. It makes passing visible without turning it into simple despair. The season leaves us listening.

question: Why does the poem not need the songs of spring?
answer: Autumn has its own beauty and music, worthy of attention without comparison to renewal.
note: Written September 1819; published 1820. Personified figures are memory aids for a non-narrative poem.

quotes.text: Season of mists and mellow fruitfulness,
quotes.context: Opening line.
quotes.meaning: The rich season begins a poem that finds value in ripeness, change and approaching decline.

title: Don Juan
author: Lord Byron
setting: Spain, the Mediterranean, Russia and England
hook: A narrator promises a hero, then carries him through scandal, shipwreck, love, and constant interruption.

characters.name: Juan
characters.role: Young traveller often acted upon by others

scenes.title: The hero is proposed
scenes.text: Byron's narrator announces Don Juan as his hero, then immediately begins commenting around him. This young man is often pursued rather than a masterful seducer. The familiar legend changes direction.
scenes.cue: THE TELLING is part of the story

scenes.title: The narrator interrupts his own hero
scenes.text: The narrator interrupts the adventure with jokes, opinions, and quarrels of his own. Following Juan means following that voice too. A straight tale keeps opening into conversation.
scenes.cue: THE NARRATOR INTERRUPTS HIS OWN HERO

scenes.title: An education meets desire
scenes.text: Juan's education does not prepare him for desire. His affair with the married Donna Julia becomes a scandal. The adults' rules and performances offer poor protection against their own contradictions.

scenes.title: The scandal gives the traveller a departure
scenes.text: His mother sends him abroad. A private scandal starts a wandering life. The departure meant to correct the young man instead launches a series of unpredictable encounters.
scenes.cue: THE SCANDAL GIVES THE TRAVELLER A DEPARTURE

scenes.title: Shipwreck strips away civilisation
scenes.text: The ship is wrecked, and survivors face hunger at sea. Social manners collapse under bodily need. The comic journey enters a scene where survival brings terrible choices.

scenes.title: Hunger strips the travellers’ manners
scenes.text: Starvation strips away claims of civilised behaviour. Juan survives while others do not. The voyage makes respectable appearances look thin beside desperate physical circumstances.

scenes.title: Haidée offers a different life
scenes.text: Washed ashore, he is rescued by Haidée and finds love with her. Their island life seems removed from the world that sent him away. A different future appears possible.

scenes.title: The island’s freedom depends upon absence
scenes.text: That freedom depends partly on her father's absence. Their happiness does not control his return. What looks like a refuge still belongs to someone with other plans.
scenes.cue: THE ISLAND’S FREEDOM DEPENDS UPON ABSENCE

scenes.title: Lambro returns
scenes.text: Lambro returns, separates the lovers, and sends Juan into slavery. Haidée dies after their separation. The idyllic interval ends through power entering the scene it had temporarily left.

scenes.title: Empires and fashionable life
scenes.text: Juan's adventures continue through a harem, war, Russia, and fashionable England. Different institutions receive the same satirical attention. Courtliness and conquest expose fresh contradictions.

scenes.title: The polished society offers another disguise
scenes.text: Polished society supplies another set of disguises for desire and ambition. Changing country does not remove hypocrisy. Juan moves while the narrator keeps recognising familiar patterns.
scenes.cue: THE POLISHED SOCIETY OFFERS ANOTHER DISGUISE

scenes.title: The narrator keeps digressing
scenes.text: The poem remains unfinished, and its voice keeps refusing a tidy road. Remember the wandering hero beside the talkative storyteller: the digressions are part of the adventure.

question: How does Byron's Juan differ from a purely active seducer?
answer: He is often acted upon and carried through circumstances, while the narrator uses his travels to satirise society.
note: Published in stages from 1819 to 1824 and left unfinished.

quotes.text: But words are things,
quotes.context: Canto III, stanza 88.
quotes.meaning: The narrator's wit also claims that language can provoke enduring consequences.

title: Goblin Market
author: Christina Rossetti
setting: A household beside a mysterious fruit market
hook: Two sisters hear fruit sellers calling, but only one discovers what their sweetness costs.

scenes.title: The merchants call
scenes.text: Two sisters, Laura and Lizzie, hear goblin merchants advertising wonderful fruit. The calls tempt them from the ordinary safety of home. Lizzie warns Laura not to listen too closely.

scenes.title: The sales pitch offers delicious certainty
scenes.text: The vendors promise delicious pleasure with inviting repetition. Nothing in the sales pitch mentions a consequence. The sisters must judge a bargain whose danger is hidden behind appetite.
scenes.cue: THE SALES PITCH OFFERS DELICIOUS CERTAINTY

scenes.title: A purchase without money
scenes.text: Laura approaches without money to pay. The goblins accept a lock of her hair. She tastes their fruit eagerly, convinced by the delight in front of her.

scenes.title: A lock of hair becomes the payment
scenes.text: A piece of her own body becomes the price. The exchange sounds small beside the feast. Only afterwards will she learn what the first taste has begun.
scenes.cue: A LOCK OF HAIR BECOMES THE PAYMENT

scenes.title: The song disappears
scenes.text: Laura wants more, but can no longer hear the goblins' call. Lizzie still hears it. Desire now reaches toward something Laura cannot find for herself.

scenes.title: Only one sister still hears the vendors
scenes.text: One sister's ears catch the market; the other's do not. Laura waits and weakens. The secret difference turns an apparently shared world into a place of isolation.
scenes.cue: ONLY ONE SISTER STILL HEARS THE VENDORS

scenes.title: The warning takes shape
scenes.text: Lizzie remembers Jeanie, another girl who ate the fruit and died. The warning has a human history. Laura's decline begins resembling a loss the sisters already know.

scenes.title: A remembered death makes the risk clearer
scenes.text: That remembered death makes delay dangerous. Lizzie cannot simply repeat her warning from a safe distance. To help her sister, she must approach the sellers herself.
scenes.cue: A REMEMBERED DEATH MAKES THE RISK CLEARER

scenes.title: Lizzie enters the market
scenes.text: She brings money and asks to buy fruit to take home. The goblins demand that she eat with them. Her refusal reveals how little their friendly offer respects a choice.

scenes.title: The rescue carries the taste
scenes.text: They attack and press fruit against her mouth, but Lizzie does not eat. Juice remains on her body. She carries that trace back as Laura's possible rescue.

scenes.title: The refusal turns invitation into assault
scenes.text: The merchants' persuasion has turned into assault. Lizzie's steadfast refusal protects her, while her willingness to enter danger gives Laura a way back from it.
scenes.cue: THE REFUSAL TURNS INVITATION INTO ASSAULT

scenes.title: The sisters remember
scenes.text: Laura consumes what Lizzie brings, suffers through the change, and recovers. Years later, the sisters tell their children. The lasting memory is of a sister who came back to help.
scenes.cue: REMEMBER who came back for you

question: What distinguishes Lizzie's visit from Laura's?
answer: Lizzie refuses the merchants' terms and acts to help her sister rather than satisfy her own craving.
note: The poem supports multiple religious, economic and gender interpretations; no single allegory exhausts it.

quotes.text: For there is no friend like a sister
quotes.context: The sisters' final lesson to their children.
quotes.meaning: The poem turns temptation and rescue into a lasting memory of mutual care.

title: Pride and Prejudice
author: Jane Austen
setting: Hertfordshire, Kent and Derbyshire
hook: An insult starts a lasting dislike, until a letter forces two proud people to look again.

scenes.title: A new neighbour changes expectations
scenes.text: At Longbourn, the Bennet family hears that wealthy Mr Bingley has rented a nearby house. Five daughters face uncertain financial futures. Their mother's hopes immediately turn toward marriage.

scenes.title: The first slight helps write the future
scenes.text: At a dance, Bingley's friend Darcy dismisses Elizabeth Bennet as insufficiently attractive. She hears of the slight and dislikes him. Their next meetings begin under that judgement.
scenes.cue: THE FIRST SLIGHT HELPS WRITE THE FUTURE

scenes.title: Charm supplies a rival account
scenes.text: The charming officer Wickham tells Elizabeth that Darcy has mistreated him. His easy manner makes the account persuasive. She now has a story that fits her existing dislike.

scenes.title: The charming witness has a motive too
scenes.text: Wickham's version hides his own conduct, including an attempted elopement with Darcy's young sister. Elizabeth does not yet know that history. Confidence has arrived ahead of sufficient evidence.
scenes.cue: THE CHARMING WITNESS HAS A MOTIVE TOO

scenes.title: Marriage has material stakes
scenes.text: Marriage offers security as well as companionship, especially when women cannot inherit the family home. Elizabeth refuses Mr Collins. Her friend Charlotte sees his offer differently.

scenes.title: Charlotte chooses within a narrower field
scenes.text: Charlotte accepts him because her options are narrower. Elizabeth struggles to understand the choice. The same marriage can look intolerable to one woman and practical to another.
scenes.cue: CHARLOTTE CHOOSES WITHIN A NARROWER FIELD

scenes.title: The first proposal fails
scenes.text: Darcy unexpectedly proposes to Elizabeth. He speaks of love while stressing the family disadvantages he has overcome. She refuses, angry at his conduct toward Jane and Wickham.

scenes.title: The proposal arrives carrying an insult
scenes.text: His proposal carries an insult inside its declaration. Elizabeth's reply forces him to hear how he appears to her. Both leave the encounter with their certainty challenged.
scenes.cue: THE PROPOSAL ARRIVES CARRYING AN INSULT

scenes.title: The letter changes the evidence
scenes.text: Darcy's letter explains Wickham's history and his own interference with Bingley. Elizabeth rereads it and reconsiders her judgement. A disliked man's evidence unsettles a charming man's story.

scenes.title: Lydia's crisis tests action
scenes.text: When Lydia elopes with Wickham, the family faces disgrace. Darcy quietly helps arrange their marriage. His behaviour during a real crisis differs from the man Elizabeth first imagined.

scenes.title: The rescue happens beyond the performance
scenes.text: He acts without presenting the rescue as a performance for Elizabeth. Learning what he has done changes her understanding further. Affection grows through evidence and changed conduct.
scenes.cue: THE RESCUE HAPPENS BEYOND THE PERFORMANCE

scenes.title: Both learn to reconsider
scenes.text: Elizabeth and Darcy meet again with greater honesty and marry. Jane and Bingley also reunite. The ending depends on people learning to revise a first impression rather than defend it forever.

question: What makes Elizabeth revise her view of Darcy?
answer: His explanatory letter and later actions reveal the weaknesses of her first impressions.

quotes.text: Till this moment I never knew myself.
quotes.context: Elizabeth, Chapter 36, after reading Darcy's letter.
quotes.meaning: The central recognition changes her judgement of both Darcy and herself.

title: Sense and Sensibility
author: Jane Austen
setting: Sussex, Devon and London
hook: Two sisters lose their home, then discover how differently a hidden promise and a public rejection can hurt.

scenes.title: The home is lost
scenes.text: When their father dies, Elinor and Marianne Dashwood lose the security of their home. Property passes to their half-brother. Their mother must begin again with a smaller income.

scenes.title: The household’s future has a smaller purse
scenes.text: A modest new household changes their expectations. Marriage, money, and affection cannot be considered separately. The sisters face uncertain futures with different habits of feeling.
scenes.cue: THE HOUSEHOLD’S FUTURE HAS A SMALLER PURSE

scenes.title: Two kinds of attachment
scenes.text: Elinor loves cautiously and conceals distress; Marianne expresses affection passionately. Each approach has strength and risk. Their stories test judgement and feeling without making either sister simple.

scenes.title: Elinor must interpret a guarded attachment
scenes.text: Elinor is drawn to Edward Ferrars, but his reserve puzzles her. She hopes his kindness means love. Something he cannot openly explain limits the future she imagines.
scenes.cue: ELINOR MUST INTERPRET A GUARDED ATTACHMENT

scenes.title: The hidden engagement
scenes.text: Lucy Steele tells Elinor that she is secretly engaged to Edward. Elinor must now endure disappointment while keeping the confidence. The hope she cannot share becomes a grief she cannot explain.
scenes.cue: RESTRAINT is not absence of pain

scenes.title: A confidence requires painful silence
scenes.text: Lucy makes Elinor her unwilling listener. Politeness and a promise of secrecy keep the pain contained. Outward composure leaves other people unaware of how much she feels.

scenes.title: A public humiliation
scenes.text: Marianne falls for the charming Willoughby, then receives a cold rejection in London. He chooses a wealthy marriage. Her openly displayed hope ends in public humiliation.

scenes.title: The charming past contains another harmed woman
scenes.text: Willoughby's past contains another woman he has harmed. Charm had hidden conduct Marianne did not know. The lover she admired must be reconsidered through what he has done.
scenes.cue: THE CHARMING PAST CONTAINS ANOTHER HARMED WOMAN

scenes.title: Brandon's history reframes the man
scenes.text: Colonel Brandon reveals that history and continues offering care. His quiet character begins to look different beside Willoughby's brilliance. Reliable action grows more significant than romantic display.

scenes.title: Illness and self-recognition
scenes.text: Marianne becomes gravely ill, and her recovery opens a period of reflection. She recognises the harm of surrendering everything to unchecked feeling. Survival gives her room to change.

scenes.title: The recovery changes how feeling is used
scenes.text: Her later affection for Brandon develops through a steadier understanding. She does not simply stop feeling deeply. She learns to join feeling with attention to another person's character.
scenes.cue: THE RECOVERY CHANGES HOW FEELING IS USED

scenes.title: The unexpected release
scenes.text: Lucy marries Edward's brother, freeing Edward from his engagement. He and Elinor marry; Marianne marries Brandon. Both sisters reach happiness after learning what their first hopes had missed.

question: Why should Elinor's restraint not be mistaken for coldness?
answer: She experiences deep pain but bears it privately and considers the needs of others.

quotes.text: I compare it with what it ought to have been
quotes.context: Marianne, Chapter 46, judging her past conduct.
quotes.meaning: Her recovery includes self-examination rather than merely exchanging one romantic attachment for another.

title: Emma
author: Jane Austen
setting: Highbury in England
hook: A confident matchmaker rearranges other people's hopes, then discovers she has misunderstood her own.

scenes.title: The matchmaker feels certain
scenes.text: In the village of Highbury, Emma Woodhouse enjoys comfort, influence, and confidence in her judgement. After a marriage she believes she helped arrange, she decides to guide another friend's future.

scenes.title: A successful match gives Emma too much confidence
scenes.text: One apparent success makes her trust her talent too much. Mr Knightley questions her interference, but she feels sure of what she sees. Harriet Smith becomes her next project.
scenes.cue: A SUCCESSFUL MATCH GIVES EMMA TOO MUCH CONFIDENCE

scenes.title: The farmer is discouraged
scenes.text: Emma discourages Harriet from accepting Robert Martin, a farmer who genuinely cares for her. She imagines a grander match. Harriet lets another person's ambition displace her own inclination.

scenes.title: Harriet’s existing affection is treated as improvable
scenes.text: The friendship gives Emma power over a young woman with less security. Raising Harriet's hopes feels generous to Emma. It also risks making a suitable, loving future seem beneath her.
scenes.cue: HARRIET’S EXISTING AFFECTION IS TREATED AS IMPROVABLE

scenes.title: Mr. Elton reveals the mistake
scenes.text: Emma assumes Mr Elton admires Harriet. His gestures actually concern Emma, and he proposes to her. The surprise exposes how confidently she has been interpreting evidence in the wrong direction.
scenes.cue: THE STORY was hers not his

scenes.title: The wrong suitor exposes the wrong reading
scenes.text: Harriet is hurt by a disappointment Emma helped create. Good intentions cannot repair it automatically. The matchmaker has to confront consequences outside her own comfortable position.
scenes.cue: THE WRONG SUITOR EXPOSES THE WRONG READING

scenes.title: Frank supplies more misdirection
scenes.text: Frank Churchill's flirtation brings further misleading appearances. Emma reads his conduct as interest in herself. His hidden relationship with Jane Fairfax makes those appearances unfair to several people.

scenes.title: The hidden engagement has serious stakes
scenes.text: Frank and Jane are secretly engaged. Jane's dependence and uncertainty give that secrecy real weight. What looks like playful social behaviour to Emma costs another woman distress.
scenes.cue: THE HIDDEN ENGAGEMENT HAS SERIOUS STAKES

scenes.title: Box Hill wounds Miss Bates
scenes.text: At Box Hill, Emma makes a cruel joke at Miss Bates's expense. Knightley rebukes her for hurting someone vulnerable. A small triumph of wit becomes a moral failure.

scenes.title: Harriet changes Emma's view
scenes.text: Harriet then admits she loves Knightley. Emma suddenly understands her own feelings for him. The observer who imagined understanding everyone else has overlooked herself.

scenes.title: A wounded neighbour needs actual attention
scenes.text: She visits Miss Bates and begins repairing the harm through attention rather than cleverness. Humility requires actual conduct. Recognising a mistake is only the beginning of making amends.
scenes.cue: A WOUNDED NEIGHBOUR NEEDS ACTUAL ATTENTION

scenes.title: Repair through attention
scenes.text: Knightley loves Emma, and they marry; Harriet returns to Robert Martin. The happy ending follows better judgement and less interference. Emma learns to look at people before arranging their lives.

question: What does the Box Hill episode teach Emma?
answer: That cleverness and privilege can become cruelty when directed at a vulnerable person.
note: Published December 1815 with a title page dated 1816.

quotes.text: She was proved to have been universally mistaken
quotes.context: Narrator, Chapter 47, as Emma confronts the consequences of her matchmaking assumptions.
quotes.meaning: Her imagination has treated guesses as knowledge; learning requires admitting that gap.

title: Jane Eyre
author: Charlotte Brontë
setting: Gateshead, Lowood, Thornfield and Ferndean
hook: An unwanted child grows into a woman who refuses love when it asks her to surrender herself.

scenes.title: The child resists humiliation
scenes.text: As a child in her aunt's house, Jane Eyre suffers rejection and punishment. She speaks back against the unfairness. Her search begins with a wish to be treated as a person.

scenes.title: The child wants justice, not merely comfort
scenes.text: She wants justice, not merely softer treatment. Anger helps her name what others expect her to endure quietly. Even before adulthood, belonging cannot mean accepting humiliation without protest.
scenes.cue: THE CHILD WANTS JUSTICE, NOT MERELY COMFORT

scenes.title: Lowood teaches and wounds
scenes.text: At Lowood school, Jane encounters harsh discipline, deprivation, and illness. Helen Burns offers friendship, and Miss Temple gives care. The institution wounds her while particular people help her grow.

scenes.title: The school’s hardship contains a different friendship
scenes.text: Helen's kindness offers another response to suffering, different from Jane's resistance. Jane loses her friend to illness. Love becomes part of the school she remembers alongside its cruelty.
scenes.cue: THE SCHOOL’S HARDSHIP CONTAINS A DIFFERENT FRIENDSHIP

scenes.title: A governess at Thornfield
scenes.text: As a governess at Thornfield, Jane teaches Adèle and meets the house's owner, Rochester. Strange laughter and unexplained disturbances trouble the building. Affection grows around an unanswered secret.

scenes.title: The employer is also a person she can answer
scenes.text: Rochester talks with Jane as someone capable of meeting his mind. Their connection crosses differences in wealth and position. She will not accept the idea that dependence makes her less human.
scenes.cue: THE EMPLOYER IS ALSO A PERSON SHE CAN ANSWER

scenes.title: The marriage is interrupted
scenes.text: They plan to marry, but the wedding is interrupted. Rochester already has a wife, Bertha Mason, confined at Thornfield. The secret changes the meaning of everything Jane has been promised.

scenes.title: The hidden wife makes the offer impossible
scenes.text: He asks Jane to remain with him despite the existing marriage. She loves him, but cannot accept the terms. A desired home now threatens the independence she has struggled to keep.
scenes.cue: THE HIDDEN WIFE MAKES THE OFFER IMPOSSIBLE

scenes.title: Jane chooses departure
scenes.text: Jane leaves without a secure destination and suffers near-starvation. The decision costs her dearly. Refusing an unequal life does not make the road afterward comfortable.

scenes.title: Another unequal offer
scenes.text: St John Rivers later offers marriage as part of his missionary vocation. Jane recognises another demand that would suppress her own feelings. She refuses duty defined entirely by someone else's plan.

scenes.title: The inheritance changes the terms of return
scenes.text: An inheritance gives Jane independence, and she shares it with her newfound relatives. She can now choose without seeking financial rescue. The terms of a possible return have changed.
scenes.cue: THE INHERITANCE CHANGES THE TERMS OF RETURN

scenes.title: Return on changed terms
scenes.text: She finds Rochester injured after Thornfield's fire, in which Bertha died. Jane returns freely and marries him. The home she chooses now rests on a different balance of dependence and care.

question: Why does Jane leave Rochester after the interrupted wedding?
answer: She refuses to sacrifice her conscience and self-respect even for a person she loves.
note: Bertha's representation and confinement raise important questions about race, disability and whose story the narrator can tell.

quotes.text: I am no bird; and no net ensnares me
quotes.context: Jane to Rochester, Chapter 23.
quotes.meaning: She asserts freedom and equal human standing within a relationship of unequal social power.

title: Wuthering Heights
author: Emily Brontë
setting: Two houses on the Yorkshire moors
hook: A rejected child grows into a man who uses property and marriage to make others share his pain.

scenes.title: The stranger hears a history
scenes.text: Visitor Lockwood arrives at Wuthering Heights and finds its household hostile and puzzling. Later, housekeeper Nelly tells him its history. The strange present begins opening through a remembered past.

scenes.title: The household is already difficult to read
scenes.text: Names, relationships, and old resentments are difficult to untangle. Lockwood's first impressions cannot explain them. The story asks us to listen through narrators who also have their own limits.
scenes.cue: THE HOUSEHOLD IS ALREADY DIFFICULT TO READ

scenes.title: An outsider in the family
scenes.text: Mr Earnshaw once brought home an orphan called Heathcliff. Catherine grew close to him, while Hindley resented the newcomer. Love and exclusion entered the same household together.

scenes.title: The child’s belonging is made insecure
scenes.text: After Earnshaw's death, Hindley degraded Heathcliff and denied him education. His place in the family became insecure. Catherine's attachment remained, but could not undo the daily humiliation.
scenes.cue: THE CHILD’S BELONGING IS MADE INSECURE

scenes.title: Catherine chooses social safety
scenes.text: Catherine chose to marry the wealthy Edgar Linton. She believed marriage to Heathcliff would lower her socially. He heard the rejection and left before hearing the fuller explanation of her bond.

scenes.title: The marriage separates two claimed identities
scenes.text: She imagined her identity inseparable from Heathcliff while marrying another man. Those claims could not easily coexist. Her decision divided social security from the attachment she considered fundamental.
scenes.cue: THE MARRIAGE SEPARATES TWO CLAIMED IDENTITIES

scenes.title: The return intensifies conflict
scenes.text: Heathcliff returned wealthy, intensifying the conflict. His marriage to Isabella and hostility toward Edgar spread the damage. Catherine became ill and died after giving birth to a daughter.

scenes.title: The returned outsider learns the uses of property
scenes.text: Heathcliff learned to use debts, inheritance, and marriage against the next generation. His revenge moved beyond the original injuries. Property could keep punishing people who had not caused them.
scenes.cue: THE RETURNED OUTSIDER LEARNS THE USES OF PROPERTY

scenes.title: The next generation is trapped
scenes.text: Young Cathy, Hareton, and Linton Heathcliff became trapped in those arrangements. Their futures served an older man's grievance. The households repeated deprivation through another set of children.

scenes.title: Learning offers another relation
scenes.text: Cathy and Hareton gradually developed kindness despite early hostility. Learning offered an alternative to domination. Their relationship could become something other than another instrument of revenge.

scenes.title: Reading creates a different kind of intimacy
scenes.text: Reading together helped change their understanding of each other. Patient attention replaced mockery. The education once denied to Heathcliff now became part of a gentler connection.
scenes.cue: READING CREATES A DIFFERENT KIND OF INTIMACY

scenes.title: The avenger loses his aim
scenes.text: Heathcliff lost his appetite for revenge and died, haunted by Catherine's memory. Cathy and Hareton planned a shared future. The ending leaves possible renewal beside the unsettled presence of the dead.

question: What makes Cathy and Hareton's relationship different?
answer: Mutual learning and affection offer a way out of the earlier pattern of humiliation and coercion.
note: The nested narration complicates certainty; the supernatural ending remains suggestive rather than conclusively explained.

quotes.text: I am Heathcliff
quotes.context: Catherine to Nelly, Chapter 9.
quotes.meaning: Her declaration makes their bond a claim about identity, even while her marriage decision divides them.

title: Great Expectations
author: Charles Dickens
setting: Kent and London
hook: A poor boy receives a fortune and guesses its source so badly that he misunderstands his own future.

scenes.title: The convict on the marsh
scenes.text: On misty marshes, young Pip encounters an escaped convict named Magwitch. Terrified, he brings the man food and a file. The frightened act begins a connection he cannot yet imagine.

scenes.title: The stolen food begins a lasting connection
scenes.text: Magwitch is caught, but protects Pip from blame. Pip returns to life with Joe, the kindly blacksmith who raises him. The marsh encounter seems finished; its consequences are not.
scenes.cue: THE STOLEN FOOD BEGINS A LASTING CONNECTION

scenes.title: Satis House creates shame
scenes.text: At Miss Havisham's decaying mansion, Pip meets Estella. She treats him with contempt for being common. The splendid, stopped world of Satis House teaches him to feel ashamed of home.
scenes.cue: DESIRE teaches him to despise home

scenes.title: The beautiful house manufactures shame
scenes.text: He mistakes refinement for worth and begins desiring a life that might make Estella love him. Miss Havisham encourages that hope without promising what he imagines.

scenes.title: The expectations arrive
scenes.text: An unnamed benefactor gives Pip money to become a gentleman in London. He assumes Miss Havisham is preparing him for Estella. The fortune arrives wrapped in his own flattering explanation.

scenes.title: The anonymous gift permits a flattering guess
scenes.text: Nobody has confirmed that explanation. Pip fills the gap with what he wants. His new life begins under a guess that shapes both ambition and disappointment.
scenes.cue: THE ANONYMOUS GIFT PERMITS A FLATTERING GUESS

scenes.title: London changes his conduct
scenes.text: In London, he spends freely and learns social manners. He also grows embarrassed by Joe. The effort to become admirable makes him less kind to someone who already loved him.

scenes.title: The gentleman becomes unkind to the loyal man
scenes.text: Joe's visit exposes the cost of Pip's shame. The gentleman cannot graciously receive the loyal blacksmith. Education and money have not yet taught him how to value affection.
scenes.cue: THE GENTLEMAN BECOMES UNKIND TO THE LOYAL MAN

scenes.title: The benefactor is revealed
scenes.text: Magwitch returns and reveals that he supplied the fortune. Pip's imagined future collapses. The money came from the convict, not from Miss Havisham's plan for Estella.

scenes.title: Care replaces disgust
scenes.text: At first repelled, Pip gradually recognises Magwitch's devotion and humanity. He tries to help him escape danger. Care begins replacing the social disgust that distorted his judgement.

scenes.title: The rescued convict becomes a human companion
scenes.text: Their attempted escape fails, and Magwitch dies with Pip beside him. Pip loses the fortune but gains a different understanding of the man. Gratitude no longer depends on respectable appearances.
scenes.cue: THE RESCUED CONVICT BECOMES A HUMAN COMPANION

scenes.title: The expectations are reconsidered
scenes.text: Joe later nurses Pip through illness. Pip repairs his loyalties and reconsiders his expectations. The closing encounter with Estella remains shaped by the novel's revised ending, not a guaranteed simple reward.
scenes.cue: WORTH is not a social costume

question: Who is Pip's actual benefactor?
answer: Magwitch, the convict Pip helped as a child, rather than Miss Havisham.
note: Serialised 1860–1861. Dickens wrote two endings; the widely printed revised ending remains open to interpretation.

quotes.text: I loved her against reason, against promise, against peace
quotes.context: Pip, Chapter 29, reflecting on Estella.
quotes.meaning: Desire keeps working against judgement and makes his hoped-for transformation painful.

title: A Tale of Two Cities
author: Charles Dickens
setting: London and Paris around the French Revolution
hook: Two men share a face, and one uses that resemblance to give the other a future.

scenes.title: A prisoner is recalled to life
scenes.text: Between London and Paris, Dr Manette returns after years imprisoned in the Bastille. His daughter Lucie helps him recover. A life thought almost lost is being recalled into human company.

scenes.title: A life is being recalled from imprisonment
scenes.text: The prison survives within his habits, including compulsive shoemaking. Release does not instantly remove its effects. Lucie's care gradually gives him a home beyond those years.
scenes.cue: A LIFE IS BEING RECALLED FROM IMPRISONMENT

scenes.title: Two men look alike
scenes.text: Charles Darnay faces trial in England, where his resemblance to Sydney Carton helps undermine identification. One face seems to appear in two men. That likeness will matter again.

scenes.title: A resemblance makes innocence harder to judge
scenes.text: The resemblance saves Darnay when appearances cannot securely distinguish him. Carton seems personally wasted beside the man he resembles. A legal coincidence opens a deeper contrast between their lives.
scenes.cue: A RESEMBLANCE MAKES INNOCENCE HARDER TO JUDGE

scenes.title: A rejected inheritance
scenes.text: Darnay rejects his French aristocratic family's cruelty and title. He hopes to live beyond their wrongdoing. Leaving an inheritance, however, cannot erase the history attached to his name.

scenes.title: A family name carries an unchosen history
scenes.text: Lucie marries Darnay, while Carton loves her without expecting marriage. He promises he would do anything for her and those she loves. The words wait for their test.
scenes.cue: A FAMILY NAME CARRIES AN UNCHOSEN HISTORY

scenes.title: Revolution answers cruelty
scenes.text: Revolution rises in France against generations of oppression. Darnay returns to help a former servant and is arrested. The family history he rejected now places him in danger.

scenes.title: The past has left a written witness
scenes.text: A written account from Dr Manette's imprisonment reveals atrocities committed by Darnay's relatives. The doctor's suffering becomes evidence inside the revolutionary court. His own words now threaten his daughter's husband.
scenes.cue: THE PAST HAS LEFT A WRITTEN WITNESS

scenes.title: The past becomes an accusation
scenes.text: Darnay is condemned through the past attached to him. Individual goodwill cannot easily answer collective vengeance. Lucie's restored family faces another separation that may become permanent.
scenes.cue: THE RECORD returns against the family

scenes.title: Carton changes the outcome
scenes.text: Carton arranges to enter Darnay's prison cell and exchange places with him. Their likeness becomes a means of escape. The man called wasted turns his life toward one decisive act.

scenes.title: The promise has to become an act
scenes.text: His promise becomes practical sacrifice as he sends Darnay back to Lucie and remains for execution. He cannot keep the family safe by words alone. Someone must occupy the condemned place.
scenes.cue: THE PROMISE HAS TO BECOME AN ACT

scenes.title: The sacrifice looks forward
scenes.text: Carton dies imagining the life his sacrifice preserves. The ending looks toward future generations rather than his own reward. The shared face leaves one man living through another's final choice.

question: What lets Carton save Darnay?
answer: Their physical resemblance allows Carton to take his place in prison and at execution.

quotes.text: It was the best of times, it was the worst of times
quotes.context: Opening sentence, Book I, Chapter 1.
quotes.meaning: The paired extremes frame an age capable of both brutal violence and extraordinary sacrifice.

title: Oliver Twist
author: Charles Dickens
setting: Workhouses and London
hook: A hungry child's request sends him through a city that keeps mistaking victims for criminals.

scenes.title: The workhouse child
scenes.text: Oliver Twist grows up in a workhouse, an institution meant to support the poor. It instead gives him hunger and harsh treatment. His childhood begins inside a system that resents his need.

scenes.title: Hunger asks an ordinary question
scenes.text: He asks for more food. The adults treat that ordinary request as outrageous rebellion. A hungry boy becomes a problem to remove rather than a person to feed.

scenes.title: Escape into another system
scenes.text: After further mistreatment, Oliver runs to London. The Artful Dodger offers welcome and takes him to Fagin. The city provides company, but the new household has another purpose.

scenes.title: A welcoming group has another use for him
scenes.text: Fagin trains boys to steal. The friendliness surrounding Oliver turns need into usefulness for a criminal group. He does not yet understand the work expected of him.
scenes.cue: A WELCOMING GROUP HAS ANOTHER USE FOR HIM

scenes.title: Brownlow offers an alternative
scenes.text: When a theft goes wrong, Mr Brownlow takes Oliver into his home. For a short time, kindness and care replace suspicion. Another way of receiving the child becomes visible.

scenes.title: The benefactor sees a person rather than a category
scenes.text: Brownlow sees an individual rather than a fixed category of poor or criminal. His trust opens a possible future. The gang fears that Oliver may expose it.
scenes.cue: THE BENEFACTOR SEES A PERSON RATHER THAN A CATEGORY

scenes.title: The gang takes him back
scenes.text: Oliver is seized and returned to Fagin's circle. Escape from the workhouse has not made him free to choose his company. Adults keep directing the path of his life.

scenes.title: A forced crime turns the victim into apparent evidence
scenes.text: Bill Sikes forces him into a burglary, during which Oliver is wounded. The victim is made to look like the offender. The household he was forced to enter later protects him.
scenes.cue: A FORCED CRIME TURNS THE VICTIM INTO APPARENT EVIDENCE

scenes.title: Nancy risks a disclosure
scenes.text: Nancy learns that Monks is plotting against Oliver and secretly tells his protectors. Helping him puts her in danger. She tries to open a door she cannot safely pass through herself.
scenes.cue: KNOWLEDGE becomes an act of care

scenes.title: Violence silences the helper
scenes.text: Sikes discovers her disclosure and murders her. The violence reveals the cost of exposing the gang. Nancy's compassion could help Oliver without rescuing her from her own situation.

scenes.title: The helper cannot escape the world she exposes
scenes.text: Her information survives even though she does not. The people defending Oliver gain the knowledge needed to challenge Monks. Care moves forward through a helper they cannot save.
scenes.cue: THE HELPER CANNOT ESCAPE THE WORLD SHE EXPOSES

scenes.title: Origins and protection
scenes.text: Oliver's origins are revealed, Monks's scheme fails, and Brownlow adopts him. The ending gives the child security. Remember how often survival depended on someone believing the person beneath the accusation.
scenes.cue: ONE RESCUE cannot justify the system

question: Why is Nancy central to Oliver's rescue?
answer: She supplies crucial information at personal risk, even though she remains trapped in the criminal world.
note: Serialised 1837–1839. Fagin's antisemitic depiction is part of the novel's historical prejudice and should be examined critically.

quotes.text: Please, sir, I want some more.
quotes.context: Oliver, Chapter 2, in the workhouse.
quotes.meaning: An ordinary request for food exposes the institution's cruelty toward a hungry child.

title: Bleak House
author: Charles Dickens
setting: London and the English countryside
hook: A court case promises an inheritance while slowly consuming the people who wait for it.

scenes.title: Fog fills the court
scenes.text: Fog hangs over London and the Court of Chancery. The inheritance case Jarndyce and Jarndyce has continued for years. Its promise holds people's futures inside an institution that never seems to finish.
scenes.cue: A SYSTEM obscures its own harm

scenes.title: The fog belongs to more than weather
scenes.text: The fog belongs to more than weather. Delays, documents, and unclear responsibilities obscure the human cost. People struggle to see a way through the system governing their hopes.
scenes.cue: THE FOG BELONGS TO MORE THAN WEATHER

scenes.title: Esther finds a household
scenes.text: Esther Summerson finds a home with John Jarndyce, alongside Richard and Ada. His kindness offers shelter from the case. The household seems capable of a different kind of care.

scenes.title: Two narrators give two kinds of seeing
scenes.text: Esther tells part of the story herself; another narrator sees beyond her knowledge. Their accounts reveal different aspects of the same world. No single viewpoint contains all its connections.
scenes.cue: TWO NARRATORS GIVE TWO KINDS OF SEEING

scenes.title: Richard waits for a fortune
scenes.text: Richard begins relying on the expected inheritance. Instead of choosing a stable profession, he returns to the lawsuit. The future fortune starts directing how he uses the present.

scenes.title: The expected inheritance begins consuming the heir
scenes.text: Legal costs and obsession wear him down. What he expects to receive gradually consumes what he already has. The case's promise becomes a form of dependence.
scenes.cue: THE EXPECTED INHERITANCE BEGINS CONSUMING THE HEIR

scenes.title: The secret mother
scenes.text: Esther discovers that Lady Dedlock is her mother. A hidden relationship connects the young woman to an aristocratic household. Secrecy has protected reputation while leaving both lives incomplete.
scenes.cue: THE PRIVATE life has a trace

scenes.title: The hidden mother faces an exposed past
scenes.text: Lady Dedlock's past becomes vulnerable to discovery. Fear of disgrace drives her from her home. The apparent security of rank cannot protect the person behind its carefully maintained appearance.
scenes.cue: THE HIDDEN MOTHER FACES AN EXPOSED PAST

scenes.title: The neglected child carries consequence
scenes.text: Jo, a neglected crossing-sweeper, links distant households through knowledge and illness. People with power repeatedly move him on. His vulnerability carries consequences beyond the place that refuses responsibility for him.

scenes.title: The search ends in loss
scenes.text: Esther searches for her mother, but finds her dead near the burial place of Esther's father. Recognition arrives without reunion. The secret has outlived the person it concealed.

scenes.title: The search loses the person it was chasing
scenes.text: The pursuit gathers people who hoped to help too late. Finding the truth cannot reopen the lost conversation. Esther must carry her mother's identity without the life together they missed.
scenes.cue: THE SEARCH LOSES THE PERSON IT WAS CHASING

scenes.title: The case consumes its prize
scenes.text: The lawsuit ends with its fortune exhausted by costs, and Richard dies. Esther builds a quieter household. The case's grand promise leaves care, rather than inheritance, as the more sustaining possession.

question: What finally happens to the money in the lawsuit?
answer: Legal costs consume the estate, destroying the promise on which Richard has built his hopes.
note: Serialised 1852–1853. Alternating narrators are central to how the novel connects personal care and systemic criticism.

quotes.text: Fog everywhere.
quotes.context: Chapter 1.
quotes.meaning: Physical fog becomes a memory image for Chancery's obscurity, delay and suffocating reach.

title: Middlemarch
author: George Eliot
setting: A provincial English town before the Reform Act
hook: People marry their hopes, then discover that the person beside them wants a different life.

scenes.title: The ideal marriage imagined
scenes.text: In provincial Middlemarch, Dorothea Brooke longs to do meaningful work. She marries the older scholar Casaubon, imagining she can help his great intellectual project. Admiration supplies what acquaintance has not yet tested.

scenes.title: The desired greatness is assigned to the wrong man
scenes.text: She assigns greatness to a man she barely understands. Marriage promises a purpose beyond ordinary comfort. Inside it, she begins discovering how much of that purpose she invented herself.
scenes.cue: THE DESIRED GREATNESS IS ASSIGNED TO THE WRONG MAN

scenes.title: A new doctor arrives
scenes.text: The young doctor Lydgate arrives with ambitions to improve medicine. He hopes professional dedication will shape his life. The town's habits and his private decisions complicate that plan.

scenes.title: The reformer also needs a household
scenes.text: He marries Rosamond Vincy, attracted by her refinement. She imagines wealth and standing; he expects sympathy for demanding work. Their shared household begins with incompatible pictures of success.
scenes.cue: THE REFORMER ALSO NEEDS A HOUSEHOLD

scenes.title: The marriage disappoints
scenes.text: Dorothea finds Casaubon jealous, limited, and unable to offer the companionship she hoped for. The marriage disappoints without making her wish to help meaningless. She has chosen its object badly.

scenes.title: The widow receives a condition disguised as protection
scenes.text: After his death, Casaubon's will threatens her inheritance if she marries Will Ladislaw. Control reaches beyond the grave. The supposed protection of a widow restricts her future choice.
scenes.cue: THE WIDOW RECEIVES A CONDITION DISGUISED AS PROTECTION

scenes.title: Another household creates pressure
scenes.text: Lydgate's debts grow, and Rosamond resists the sacrifices he proposes. Financial pressure exposes their different priorities. Neither person's imagined marriage can comfortably contain the other's.

scenes.title: The shared marriage contains different desired futures
scenes.text: Their disputes reveal how affection can coexist with misunderstanding. The household affects the doctor's public ambition. Work and private life do not remain separate worlds.
scenes.cue: THE SHARED MARRIAGE CONTAINS DIFFERENT DESIRED FUTURES

scenes.title: The past enters the town
scenes.text: The banker Bulstrode's concealed past emerges and draws Lydgate into suspicion. Reputation becomes a town-wide force. People make judgements through partial knowledge and existing rivalries.

scenes.title: Dorothea sees another person's pain
scenes.text: Dorothea reaches toward Rosamond with sympathy, despite pain caused by what she thinks she has seen. Her willingness to consider another person's suffering changes the encounter.

scenes.title: Sympathy must pass through an injured first impression
scenes.text: She has to move beyond an injured first impression to listen. Compassion does not come from ignorance of hurt. It comes from making room for a life beyond her own explanation.
scenes.cue: SYMPATHY MUST PASS THROUGH AN INJURED FIRST IMPRESSION

scenes.title: Lives continue beyond their hopes
scenes.text: Dorothea chooses Will and a less grand future; other lives settle with mixed gains and losses. The novel values small, often unseen acts whose effects continue beyond frustrated ambitions.
scenes.cue: UNRECORDED care also changes the world

question: What connects Dorothea's and Lydgate's stories?
answer: Idealistic ambitions are constrained by mistaken marriages, money and the needs of other people.
note: Published in parts 1871–1872. Multiple plots interlock; these frames follow two central strands.

quotes.text: the growing good of the world
quotes.context: Finale, the narrator's judgement of Dorothea's less visible influence.
quotes.meaning: Lives without public greatness can still sustain the welfare of others.

title: The Mill on the Floss
author: George Eliot
setting: Dorlcote Mill and St. Ogg’s
hook: A bright girl seeks room to live, while her brother keeps drawing the boundaries tighter.

characters.name: Tom Tulliver
characters.role: Brother committed to duty and respectability

scenes.title: The siblings inhabit different worlds
scenes.text: Beside the River Floss, Maggie and Tom Tulliver grow up in the same family but receive different expectations. Maggie is imaginative and eager; Tom prizes rules and practical certainty.

scenes.title: The bright girl needs more room than she receives
scenes.text: Her intelligence needs opportunities the household does not readily offer. What makes her lively can also make her troublesome in other people's eyes. Affection comes with demands to be smaller.
scenes.cue: THE BRIGHT GIRL NEEDS MORE ROOM THAN SHE RECEIVES

scenes.title: The family loses its footing
scenes.text: Their father loses a lawsuit and the family's mill. Financial ruin narrows both children's futures. An adult quarrel now determines the boundaries of the younger generation's lives.
scenes.cue: A DEBT becomes a family boundary

scenes.title: An adult quarrel becomes the children’s boundary
scenes.text: Mr Tulliver's hostility toward lawyer Wakem passes to Tom. Maggie's friendship with Wakem's son Philip becomes forbidden. The children inherit a conflict they did not choose.
scenes.cue: AN ADULT QUARREL BECOMES THE CHILDREN’S BOUNDARY

scenes.title: Renunciation promises peace
scenes.text: Maggie turns toward self-denial, hoping it can quiet her desires and make suffering bearable. Renunciation seems to offer order when her wishes keep meeting opposition.
scenes.cue: SUPPRESSION is not an easy cure

scenes.title: Renunciation promises a way to quiet desire
scenes.text: She tries to live by reducing what she asks from the world. Yet feelings do not disappear simply because she distrusts them. The effort at peace contains another struggle.
scenes.cue: RENUNCIATION PROMISES A WAY TO QUIET DESIRE

scenes.title: Philip understands her
scenes.text: Philip understands her imagination and offers companionship. Their secret meetings give Maggie room to speak. Tom's demand that she end the connection closes that possibility again.

scenes.title: The boat takes a hesitation beyond easy recall
scenes.text: Later, Maggie joins Stephen Guest on a boat. Their mutual attraction carries the journey farther than intended. Physical movement turns hesitation into a situation harder to reverse.
scenes.cue: THE BOAT TAKES A HESITATION BEYOND EASY RECALL

scenes.title: Stephen brings another temptation
scenes.text: Stephen is attached to Maggie's cousin Lucy. He offers a future that would hurt others. Maggie must choose between an intense feeling and obligations she cannot honestly dismiss.
scenes.cue: DESIRE puts other lives at risk

scenes.title: The return is judged
scenes.text: She returns rather than marry him, but her community judges her harshly. The decision to avoid one wrong does not protect her from suspicion about what already happened.
scenes.cue: CHOOSING rightly may not restore reputation

scenes.title: The return asks for a difficult kind of courage
scenes.text: Maggie faces rejection, including Tom's, while trying to stand by her choice. Returning requires courage without promising acceptance. The home she approaches is not automatically a refuge.
scenes.cue: THE RETURN ASKS FOR A DIFFICULT KIND OF COURAGE

scenes.title: The flood reunites them
